presentations.convener: Nobuhito MORI (Kyoto University) mori.nobuhito.8a@kyoto-u.ac.jp
presentations.session_chairs: Hai Van DANG (Hanyang University)
presentations.presentation_title: Wave Attenuation by Rhizophora Mangroves Using a Fully Nonlinear Boussinesq Model
presentations.institution: National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
presentations.abstract: Mangroves play a critical role in coastal protection by effectively attenuating wave energy during extreme events, such as tsunamis and storm surges. However, the accurate numerical representation of wave-vegetation interaction remains a significant challenge. This study integrates a vegetation module into a fully nonlinear Boussinesq model, FUNWAVE-VEG (Fully Nonlinear Boussinesq WAVE Model-VEGetation), and evaluates two distinct modeling strategies: (1) the perturbation velocity approach and (2) the reference velocity approach. The perturbation velocity approach simulates vegetation-induced resistance by extending horizontal velocities vertically, enabling the incorporation of self-specified vegetation morphologies—crucial for representing the complex prop roots of Rhizophora mangrove species. In contrast, the reference velocity approach offers higher computational efficiency by utilizing flow velocities at a specific reference level derived from depth-averaged properties. Both approaches were validated against experimental wave flume data. The results demonstrate the trade-offs between vertical resolution and computational demand, providing a robust numerical framework for predicting wave damping in coastal ecosystems. This paper will discuss the detailed implementation and comparative performance of these two approaches at AOGS 2026 in Fukuoka.

presentations.presentation_title: Predictions of Extreme Sea Levels Under Climate Change
presentations.abstract: Accurate projections of future extreme sea levels (ESLs) are urgently needed to inform coastal adaptation planning under climate change, as rising mean sea levels and intensifying storm regimes jointly threaten to drastically elevate coastal flooding risks. Traditional stationary statistical models, which assume constant climatic conditions, have become inadequate for capturing these accelerating and interdependent changes. This study addresses this critical methodological gap by developing and applying a non-stationary extreme value analysis framework that jointly models long-term sea-level rise (SLR) and time-varying storm characteristics, including storm intensity, frequency, and associated surge behavior. To achieve this, we integrate multi-decadal tide-gauge observations with ensemble projections of SLR and dynamically downscaled storm scenarios from global climate models, considering multiple future emission pathways. The non-stationary model explicitly accounts for temporal trends in both mean sea level and storm-related extremes, enabling a more realistic representation of their combined influence under changing climatic conditions. Our results reveal that ESLs are projected to increase substantially across all study regions by 2100. While SLR remains the dominant driver, changes in storm activity amplify extreme water levels significantly, contributing an additional 10-40% to ESLs in certain vulnerable regions, such as subtropical coastlines exposed to tropical cyclones. Under high-emission scenarios, water levels historically considered 100-year events are projected to recur every 1-10 years by the end of the century. This dramatic shortening of return periods reflects a nonlinear escalation in coastal hazard frequency, with profound implications for infrastructure, ecosystems, and communities. These findings underscore the pressing need to transition from stationary to dynamic, non-stationary risk assessment frameworks that integrate both SLR and storm variability.

presentations.session_title: Ocean Mixing and Internal Wave
presentations.convener: Zhenhua XU (Chinese Academy of Sciences) xuzhenhua@qdio.ac.cn
presentations.session_chairs: Zhenhua XU (Chinese Academy of Sciences) , Yuki TANAKA (Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology) , Robin ROBERTSON (Xiamen University Malaysia) , Dmitrii STEPANOV (V.I. Il'ichev Pacific Oceanological Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences)
presentations.presentation_title: Parameterization of Near-inertial-wave Induced Mixing Under the Influence of Mesoscale Eddies
presentations.institution: South China Sea Institute of Oceanology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: Near-inertial waves (NIWs) are an important source of ocean mixing and their proper parameterization in eddy-permitting ocean models is crucial for a variety of processes. Existing parameterization schemes have not considered the influence of background mesoscale eddies. By using mooring data, shipborne turbulence microstructure measurements, reanalysis data, and a slab model, we develop a new NIW-induced mixing parameterization scheme that takes into account the influence of background mesoscale eddies. The development process consists of four steps: (1) determining the upper mixed layer depth using a critical Richardson number criterion; (2) quantifying wind power input into NIWs; (3) calculating near-inertial energy flux through the bottom of the upper mixed layer; (4) determining the vertical dissipation structure in the ocean interior. Shipborne turbulent microstructure profiles are utilized to validate the proposed new scheme. It is found that, by applying this new parameterization scheme, the root-mean-squared error of log10(kappa), where kappa is the parameterized diffusivity, is reduced by 28%-37% and 27%-53% under negative and positive background vorticity, respectively. This shows a significant improvement of the present new scheme over the existing scheme, which applies to both negative and positive background vorticities.

presentations.presentation_title: Modulation of Diurnal and Semi-diurnal Internal Tides by Mesoscale Eddies and Background Currents in the Philippine Sea
presentations.abstract: This study investigates how mesoscale eddies and background currents modulate the generation and propagation of internal tides in the Philippine Sea using observations from pressure-sensor-equipped inverted echo sounders (PIES). Diurnal internal tides generated in the Luzon Strait propagate ~2,100 km to the PIES observation sites centered near 17°N, 141°E. Their amplitudes weaken during summer, in contrast to the semi-annual variability of the barotropic diurnal tide. The propagation paths of these tides exhibit seasonal equatorward refraction, with stronger refraction occurring in summer when upstream relative vorticity is negative, indicating that anticyclonic mesoscale eddies enhance equatorward refraction during this period. Semi-diurnal internal tides are generated near the Mariana Arc, where arc-shaped topography induces ray-path convergence toward a focal region. Their variability is controlled by the semi-annual cycle of the barotropic tide, variations in background zonal currents, and changes in the strength of ray-path convergence. During La Niña and negative Pacific Decadal Oscillation phases, southward shifts of the North Equatorial Current intensify the influence of the eastward-flowing Subtropical Countercurrent, enhancing both the generation and focusing of semi-diurnal internal tides. Our results demonstrate that both diurnal and semi-diurnal internal tides efficiently transport energy from their generation regions into the deep ocean, with their variability strongly influenced by background circulation and large-scale climate variability.

presentations.convener: Zhenhua XU (Chinese Academy of Sciences) xuzhenhua@qdio.ac.cn
presentations.session_chairs: Zhenhua XU (Chinese Academy of Sciences) , Yuki TANAKA (Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology) , Robin ROBERTSON (Xiamen University Malaysia) , Dmitrii STEPANOV (V.I. Il'ichev Pacific Oceanological Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences)
presentations.presentation_title: Interannual Variability of Deep Cycle Turbulence in the Equatorial Pacific
presentations.abstract: In the equatorial region, turbulence in the upper ocean exhibits a vertical cycle associated with the diurnal cycle of solar radiation, known as the deep cycle (DC). It arises as trade-wind-induced shear is confined near the surface by daytime solar heating, whereas nighttime surface cooling allows turbulence to descend below the mixed-layer base via marginal instability until solar heating resumes. Because DC can influence large-scale phenomena such as the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) through vertical mixing, studying DC is important for understanding ENSO mechanisms and the climate system. However, the interannual variability of DC remains largely unexplored, partly due to limited observations. In this study, deep-cycle turbulence (DCT) in the equatorial Pacific is simulated using a regional ocean model, and its characteristics are compared among different ENSO periods. The model reproduces the essential observed features of DCT, despite some differences in the simulated background fields. The results also show that DCT on the equator at 140°W is more intense and penetrates deeper during El Niño Modoki events, which is likely related to a deeper thermocline and strengthened trade winds in the eastern equatorial Pacific. In contrast, DCT in January 1998, around the peak phase of the 1997-98 canonical El Niño, is much weaker than during El Niño Modoki and La Niña events, partly due to weaker trade winds. These results suggest that DCT characteristics vary not only among ENSO phases but also among different El Niño types.

presentations.convener: Zhenhua XU (Chinese Academy of Sciences) xuzhenhua@qdio.ac.cn
presentations.session_chairs: Zhenhua XU (Chinese Academy of Sciences) , Yuki TANAKA (Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology) , Robin ROBERTSON (Xiamen University Malaysia) , Dmitrii STEPANOV (V.I. Il'ichev Pacific Oceanological Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences)
presentations.presentation_title: Exploring a New Parameterization for Abyssal Tide-induced Near-field Mixing
presentations.presenting_author: Toshiyuki Hibiya (Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology (JAMSTEC))
presentations.abstract: Deep ocean mixing plays a fundamental role in regulating the strength and structure of the meridional overturning circulation. Turbulent mixing in the deep ocean is commonly classified into two regimes: far-field mixing in the ocean interior and near-field mixing near ocean boundaries. While the physical mechanisms governing far-field mixing have been extensively investigated and adequately parameterized (Wijesekera et al., 1993; Gregg et al., 2003; Ijichi and Hibiya, 2015), near-field mixing remains poorly understood due to the difficulty of direct microstructure observations. Near-field mixing is generally more intense than far-field mixing, highlighting the need for improved physical understanding and parameterization. Motivated by this challenge, Hibiya and colleagues theoretically investigated near-field mixing generated above rough seafloor topography (Hibiya, 2022; Hibiya et al., 2017, 2024). Their numerical experiments demonstrated that when tidal currents intensify such that the tidal excursion parameter Te=kHUB/ω>1 with kH the horizontal wavenumber of the seafloor topography, UB the semidiurnal tidal velocity amplitude, and ω its frequency, high-frequency internal lee waves—rather than internal tides as previously assumed—are generated and propagate upward. These internal lee waves interact with a background Garrett-Munk-like internal wave field, producing localized mixing hotspots above the seafloor. Furthermore, they showed that the vertical extent of these mixing hotspots depends strongly on the steepness parameter Sp=Nh0/UB with N the buoyancy frequency and h0 the topographic amplitude. When Sp < 0.2, breaking of internal lee waves forms tall mixing hotspots, whereas for Sp > 0.2, near-inertial shear over the seafloor topography suppresses upward propagation of internal lee waves, resulting in short mixing hotspots. However, the physical mechanisms responsible for this strong dependence on Sp remain unclear. Here, we investigate how the temporal evolution of near-inertial shear over seafloor topography depends on Sp. Building on these results, we propose a physically motivated parameterization for near-field mixing.

presentations.presentation_title: Mooring Observed Seasonal Variability of Internal Tides Radiated from Mariana Arc
presentations.abstract: Seasonal variability of the magnitude and structure of semidiurnal internal tides radiated from the Mariana Arc was examined based on year-long mooring observations. Internal tidal currents, energy density, and energy flux at the focal point of the Mariana Arc were weakest in summer, but typically comparable in the other three seasons. Mode-1 internal tides dominate over the observed period, except in summer when Mode-2 explains a higher proportion. The coherent variance accounts for about 60% of the total semidiurnal motions, with a reduced proportion in summer and winter, generally consistent with the seasonal trend of the barotropic tides. In contrast, the incoherent internal tides show a close temporal consistency with the low-frequency flows. During summer, the background currents are predominantly influenced by energetic mesoscale eddies, whereas the North Equatorial Current (NEC) system dominates in the other seasons. Internal tides influenced by eddies exhibit more standing wave characteristics, higher modal structures, and more incoherent properties compared to those modulated by the NEC. Internal tides are more progressive and propagate outward more easily when modulated by the NEC, whereas those modulated by eddies are more unstable and prone to nearby dissipation, resulting in a significant summer weakening at the Mariana Arc focus.

presentations.session_title: Coastal Hazards: Impacts of Tropical Storms and Tsunamis
presentations.convener: Nobuhito MORI (Kyoto University) mori.nobuhito.8a@kyoto-u.ac.jp
presentations.session_chairs: Philip Li-Fan LIU (Texas A&M University) , Yuchen WANG (Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology)
presentations.presentation_title: Numerical Simulation and Regional Characteristic Analysis of Multi-source Earthquake Tsunamis in the Curved Subduction System in Southeast Asia
presentations.abstract: The curved subduction system in Southeast Asia is one of the world's most seismically and tsunamigenically active regions. Its extensive coastline, high exposure, and dense population further exacerbate the tsunami risk. The earthquake tsunami source system in this region is structurally complex, such as megathrusts, fore-arc detachment faults, and back-arc thrust faults. However, compared with the tsunami research in the western Indonesia, existing tsunami research in this region remains fragmented, lacking a holistic, systematic analysis of tsunami characteristics from multiple earthquake sources within the curved subduction system. This study sorted out and constructed potential tsunamigenic sources, encompassing megathrusts, fore-arc detachment faults, and back-arc thrust faults. The work primarily includes: (1) Utilizing the COMCOT model for tsunami simulations to reveal the generation and propagation characteristics of tsunamis within this complex tectonic system from an integrated perspective; (2) Conducting a comparative analysis of the differences in tsunami features generated by various sources (e.g., megathrusts, intraplate thrust faults, detachment faults), with a focus on clarifying the systematic distinctions in their affected areas; (3) Comparing the results with tsunami cases from other global subduction zones to summarize the controlling factors for key characteristics such as arrival times (e.g., the extremely short arrival time for tsunamis generated along the Java subduction zone), thereby elucidating the unique aspects of tsunami propagation in this region. This research aims to provide a more comprehensive perspective for regional tsunami hazard analysis and a deepened understanding of disaster mechanisms within curved subduction systems.

presentations.session_title: Coastal Hazards: Impacts of Tropical Storms and Tsunamis
presentations.convener: Nobuhito MORI (Kyoto University) mori.nobuhito.8a@kyoto-u.ac.jp
presentations.session_chairs: Philip Li-Fan LIU (Texas A&M University) , Yuchen WANG (Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology)
presentations.presentation_title: Physics-based Modeling of Tsunami Hazard Variability in the Gulf of Aqaba
presentations.institution: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Situated at the northeastern end of the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aqaba is the seismically most active region in Saudi Arabia and forms a narrow, deep, and semi-enclosed coastal water body between the Sinai and Arabian peninsulas. Beyond seismic hazard, historical records and recent studies indicate that tsunamis generated by earthquakes and landslides have occurred in the region, posing a potential threat to nearby coastal communities. However, limited observational data hinder a comprehensive understanding of tsunami source processes and the resulting hazards in the region. Rapid coastal development, including the infrastructural giga-project NEOM in the vicinity of the Gulf of Aqaba in Saudi Arabia, together with continued expansion of tourism along the coastlines, further underscores the need for improved tsunami hazard assessment in the Gulf of Aqaba region. In this study, we conduct a suite of dynamic simulations of mechanically plausible earthquake and landslide scenarios in the Gulf of Aqaba and their associated tsunamis. The results indicate that, for earthquake sources, variations in rupture nucleation location exert a strong control on rupture extent, generating events of up to Mw 7.6 with differing tsunami impacts. Rupture directivity further modulates localized tsunami hazard, while time-dependent seafloor deformation plays a critical role in tsunami generation and propagation. Simulations of landslide-generated tsunamis demonstrate a strong sensitivity of tsunami excitation to landslide thickness, source volume, and material properties. In particular, the solid volume fraction and permeability emerge as key controls on tsunami generation efficiency, with contractive, low-permeability slides producing substantially larger waves than non-contractive, high-permeability counterparts. Moreover, the narrow and semi-enclosed geometry of the Gulf promotes wave resonance and reduces energy dissipation, leading to persistent seiche effects that amplify tsunami hazard along coastal communities. These findings underscore the importance of accounting for tsunami source characteristics and dynamics, highlighting the necessity of scenario-based, physics-driven hazard assessments.

presentations.presentation_title: From Summit to Seafloor: Quantifying the Source of the 1871 Ruang Volcano Tsunami Through Integrated Dem and Bathymetry Analysis
presentations.abstract: The 1871 eruption of Ruang Volcano in the Sangihe Islands, Indonesia, generated a destructive tsunami, causing over 400 deaths on the neighbouring island of Tagulandang. The cause of the tsunami is not well constrained, which has prevented accurate modelling of the event and the assessment of future volcanic tsunami risk. Here, we present new field, archival and remote-sensing observations from the event, identifying the most likely source as a flank landslide from the northern sector of Ruang’s summit. The mass balance between the onshore landslide and offshore deposits helps constrain the source volume and the volume that entered the sea, an essential step to accurately modelling the tsunami. This study integrates topographic and bathymetric data to quantify the spatial extent and volume of the 1871 collapse and associated submarine deposition. A pre-event digital elevation model (DEM) was reconstructed by restoring the missing flank morphology based on remnants of older surfaces and slope continuity, while a post-event surface was obtained by removing younger volcanic infill. The difference between these surfaces defines the subaerial failure volume. Bathymetric data around Ruang and the strait toward Tagulandang were analyzed to identify mounds and depressions consistent with the deposit area, showing the presence of thickened, lobate and mounded features interpreted as submarine deposits formed in the 1871 event. Preliminary results indicate that consistency between the submerged deposits and an identified landslide source region. This has been used to model the event and test if this landslide volume can generate tsunami impacts consistent with the observed impacts of the event. only part of the failed material entered the sea. This integrated DEM and bathymetry approach provides new quantitative constraints on the 1871 Ruang collapse and contributes to understanding volcanic tsunami coupling in the Sangihe Arc.

presentations.convener: Nobuhito MORI (Kyoto University) mori.nobuhito.8a@kyoto-u.ac.jp
presentations.session_chairs: Philip Li-Fan LIU (Texas A&M University) , Yuchen WANG (Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology)
presentations.presentation_title: Eruption Forcing and Tsunami Response in the 2022 Hunga Tonga Event
presentations.abstract: The January 15, 2022 eruption of the Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai (HTHH) submarine volcano produced one of the most powerful volcanic events in recent history, generating global shock waves and tsunamis observed across the Pacific. While far-field tsunami signals have been attributed to atmospheric Lamb and gravity waves, the near-field tsunami that struck Tongatapu caused run-up heights exceeding 10 m and severe inundation. Its generation mechanism remains unclear, as static initial displacement models have failed to reproduce observed inundation and run-up. This study applies a time-dependent vertical forcing model to investigate the near-field tsunami. A coupled framework was employed: CADMAS-SURF/3D was used to simulate eruption-driven vertical water motion, and the results were transferred to STOC-ML for regional propagation. Two source models were compared. In static displacement cases, prescribed uplift patterns reproduced some waveforms but underestimated inundation, especially along the northwestern coast of Tongatapu. In dynamic cases, vertical velocities of 5–20 m/s were imposed at the caldera. Results showed strong dependence on input velocity. The 10 m/s case reproduced both the inundation extent and run-up heights observed in post-event surveys, whereas lower velocities underestimated and higher velocities overestimated impacts. The findings highlight the essential role of time-dependent forcing in volcanic tsunami generation. Unlike static models, dynamic forcing transfers momentum realistically, enabling accurate reproduction of observed inundation. This approach provides a quantitative link between eruption dynamics and tsunami impacts and underscores the need to incorporate source time functions into volcanic tsunami hazard assessment.

presentations.session_chairs: Philip Li-Fan LIU (Texas A&M University) , Yuchen WANG (Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology)
presentations.presentation_title: Re-examination of the 1952 Kamchatka Earthquake Source Model Using Tsunami Waveforms and Calibrations from the 2025 Kamchatka Earthquake
presentations.abstract: The earthquake that occurred on the plate interface offshore Kamchatka on 29 July 2025 gives an opportunity to re-estimate the source of the 1952 Kamchatka megathrust earthquake. There is still no clear explanation for how the two interplate earthquakes rupture the same plate interface within only 73 years, which is a short time span to accumulate enough strain energy for the recent event. Both earthquakes generated Pacific wide tsunamis, however, the 1952 event lacks the quality and quantity of data available for the 2025 event. Tsunami waveforms from the 2025 earthquake, recorded by offshore DART buoy stations, are used to estimate fault slip distribution. The estimated seismic moment from the model is 1.13 × 1022 Nm (Mw 8.6), with a major slip region about 50 km long located at depths of ~30 km. Time-shift and amplitude-scaling parameters are derived by fitting observed coastal tsunami waveforms to simulations based on this reference model. These correction parameters allow the inversion to produce a reliable slip distribution of the 1952 earthquake. This model gives a seismic moment of the 1952 earthquake is 2.01 × 1022 Nm (Mw 8.8) and suggests a rupture that extended to the shallow plate interface near the trench.

presentations.convener: Nobuhito MORI (Kyoto University) mori.nobuhito.8a@kyoto-u.ac.jp
presentations.session_chairs: Philip Li-Fan LIU (Texas A&M University) , Yuchen WANG (Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology)
presentations.presentation_title: Constraining Tsunami Hazard from Submarine Landslides Off Northwest Borneo Using Volume-dependent Scenarios
presentations.abstract: Previous bathymetric and seismic surveys in the South China Sea have identified a massive historical submarine landslide, known as the Brunei Slide, off the coast of Brunei. While several attempts have been made to assess the associated tsunami hazard, these studies are highly localised to specific locations around East Malaysia and Brunei. The hazard to the wider Southeast Asian region is still largely unconstrained. Addressing this knowledge gap, this study presents the first regional hazard assessment to examine the potential tsunami threat from submarine mass flow events similar to the Brunei Slide. We adopt a two-part coupled modeling approach, using the Non-Hydrostatic Wave Model (NHWAVE) and the Fully Nonlinear Boussinesq Wave Model (FUNWAVE), and consider a wider range of landslide volumes (600, 900, 1200, 1500, and 1800 km3) to account for smaller, more plausible events and the larger, more extreme events. We find that, in addition to East Malaysia and Brunei, other regional areas such as the Riau Islands (Indonesia) and Vietnam may also experience an elevated coastal hazard, with maximum amplitudes exceeding 2 m under the smallest volume scenario of 600 km3. While proximity plays a critical role in shaping the regional hazard distribution, it cannot fully explain the observed local variations. Additional factors such as the gradient and shape of the continental slope, as well as the presence of islands and coral reefs, are likely to exert significant influence in the local context. Finally, we find that maximum amplitudes scale linearly with volumetric changes. Although heteroscedasticity warrants further investigation, this relationship offers valuable insights for advancing our understanding of landslide-generated tsunami hazards in the region.

presentations.presentation_title: Tsunami Warning Cancellation Based on Data Assimilation with a Nonlinear Propagation Model: Application to the 2025 Mw 8.8 Kamchatka Earthquake
presentations.institution: Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: On 29 July 2025, an Mw 8.8 megathrust earthquake occurred off the eastern coast of the Kamchatka Peninsula. The earthquake generated a large tsunami that reached Japan approximately 2 h later, with a maximum observed height of ~1.3 m. Offshore observation networks have been deployed in Japan: S-net, DONET, and N-net. These networks are equipped with bottom pressure sensors that record water pressure in real time, enabling tsunami detection before waves reach the coast. Offshore observations can be adopted to predict coastal tsunamis based on data assimilation approach, which has been successfully validated using linear propagation models. Although linear models can accurately predict tsunami arrival, they are less capable of forecasting the tsunami decay process (i.e., following waves). The 2025 Kamchatka earthquake tsunami was the largest event since the completion of S-net, providing an opportunity to extend the data assimilation framework to a nonlinear formulation. We applied a nonlinear propagation model that accounts for advection and bottom friction, using S-net observations as the inputs for data assimilation. The objective was to predict tsunami arrival and decay process. The Tohoku region of Japan was selected as the study area, and the tsunami was predicted up to 24 h after the earthquake. Results show that data assimilation approach enables accurate predictions of tsunami heights at least 30 min before its arrival. Linear and nonlinear models perform comparably in predicting tsunami arrival. However, for the following wave prediction, the linear model tends to diverge due to numerical instabilities, whereas the nonlinear model more reliably captures decay process. The nonlinear model achieved prediction accuracy of 60–80% across eight tide gauges, with an average RMSE between observed and forecasted waveforms of <0.1 m. These results demonstrate that nonlinear data assimilation facilitates more reliable following wave prediction, thereby supporting tsunami warning cancellation.

presentations.session_title: Multiscale Variabilities in the Western Pacific Ocean and Their Impacts on Multi-disciplinary Aspects
presentations.convener: Akira NAGANO (Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology) nagano@jamstec.go.jp
presentations.session_chairs: Hanna NA (Seoul National University) , Linlin ZHANG (Institute of Oceanology, Chinese Academy of Sciences)
presentations.presentation_title: Interdecadal Variability of Marine Cold Spells in the Taiwan Strait During 1985 and 2025
presentations.institution: Third Institute of Oceanography, Ministry of Natural Resources
presentations.abstract: Despite a global decline in marine cold spells (MCSs) under ongoing warming, the Taiwan Strait shows an anomalous increase in wintertime MCS frequency and persistence since 2010, causing large-scale coral cold-bleaching and fishery decline. This study investigates the interdecadal variability and physical mechanisms of wintertime MCSs in the Taiwan Strait from 1985 to 2025 using multi-source satellite observations and reanalysis data. Results reveal a clear transition around 2010. Before 2010, MCSs occurred only about 0.5 events per year and lasted ~33 days on average. After 2010, both frequency and duration nearly doubled to 1.1 events per year and ~55 days. Mixed-layer heat budget diagnostics show that this shift is closely tied to changes in the East Asian Winter Monsoon (EAWM), the China Coastal Current (CCC), and Kuroshio intrusion. In the earlier period, MCS development was dominated by surface thermodynamic cooling, with latent and sensible heat fluxes accounting for 91% of the mixed-layer tendency, while horizontal advection contributed only 13%; warm advection from a stronger Kuroshio intrusion also offset nearshore cooling. After 2010, the intensified and more persistent EAWM altered the relative contributions of cooling processes: cold-water advection by the strengthened CCC increased to 28%, while a weakened and contracted Kuroshio intrusion enhanced cold anomalies and prolonged event duration. This interdecadal transition reflects a shift from a primarily surface-flux–driven regime to a coupled thermodynamic–dynamic regime. Further analyses suggest this transition may be associated with the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO).

presentations.presentation_title: Impact of a Wintertime Marine Heatwave on a Heavy Rainfall Event in Northern Japan in January 2024
presentations.abstract: Since the spring of 2023, the Kuroshio Extension has shifted northward and is located immediately east of northern Japan, leading to a marine heat wave (MHW). Although several previous studies have investigated the impact of MHWs on weather during the warm season, only a few studies have investigated their impact during wintertime. This study focused on a heavy rainfall event along the eastern coast of Tohoku District in northern Japan that occurred on January 21, 2024, which was caused by a low-pressure system moving along the southern coast of Japan. During this event, the daily precipitation in January was the highest in the recorded history at several observation points in Tohoku. The MHW located to the east of northern Japan may have increased the rainfall amounts because southeasterly winds, which were associated with the low-pressure system and brought heavy rainfall, passed over the MHW before reaching Tohoku. Regional atmospheric model experiments confirmed that the MHW off the coast of Tohoku increased the rainfall amounts along the Tohoku coast through increasing the moisture flux from over the MHW to Tohoku. This increase was likely due to the stronger winds that were associated with the decreased sea level pressures over the MHW. While snow generally occurs in Tohoku in winter, rain occurred in this case because of the increased air temperatures, potentially impacting agricultural and social activities. The findings of this study contribute to our understanding of how wintertime MHWs affect weather.

presentations.presentation_title: Mesoscale Cyclonic Eddies Inject Nutrient to the Kuroshio Recirculation Gyre
presentations.institution: Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Although surface layers of the western North Pacific subtropical gyre, where the Kuroshio Current flows along its northwestern rims, are known to be nutrient-poor, the Kuroshio and Kuroshio Extension regions are one of the major CO2 sinks for the atmosphere. On the other hand, subsurface layers of the Kuroshio carry nutrients from the south to the Kuroshio Extension region as a nutrient stream, which can be supplied to the euphotic layer to promote the biological pump and CO2 uptake by the ocean. Previous studies have shown that the high primary production and carbon export flux in the Kuroshio recirculation gyre are attributed to the mesoscale cyclonic eddies. However, because of the lack of direct turbulence measurements within cyclonic eddies, it remains unclear how much nutrients can be injected into the Kuroshio recirculation gyre. In this study, data obtained from a tow-yo microstructure profiler within a cyclonic eddy during July 2019 R/V Hakuho-Maru cruise were examined to quantify diffusive nitrate flux. In addition, using a triple-decomposition framework, lateral flux of nitrate from the cyclonic eddy to ambient water is estimated. Furthermore, mesoscale cyclonic eddies in the Kuroshio recirculation gyre are detected and tracked using a 2-km resolution ocean reanalysis product. The results indicate that turbulence is enhanced in the uplifted pycnocline at the center of the cyclonic eddy, where clear subsurface chlorophyll-a maxima appear, resulting in large vertical nitrate diffusive fluxes of 0.1-1m-2 day-1. The integrated diffusive nitrate flux within the eddy is estimated to be 1.6 M mol day-1. The eddy tracking results indicate that 1-2 cyclonic eddies are propagating in the Kuroshio recirculation gyre, which are generated from the Kuroshio Extension around 145-155°E, propagate southwestward to the Kuroshio recirculation gyre, and often return northward to the Kuroshio Extension.

presentations.session_title: Multiscale Variabilities in the Western Pacific Ocean and Their Impacts on Multi-disciplinary Aspects
presentations.convener: Akira NAGANO (Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology) nagano@jamstec.go.jp
presentations.session_chairs: Hanna NA (Seoul National University) , Linlin ZHANG (Institute of Oceanology, Chinese Academy of Sciences)
presentations.presentation_title: First Dataset of Dissolved Inorganic Radiocarbon in North Pacific Subtropical Mode Water
presentations.abstract: The formation of North Pacific Subtropical Mode Water (STMW) plays a crucial role in redistributing carbon and nutrients in the North Pacific (NP) Ocean. Previous studies suggest that STMW supplies nutrients from the subsurface to the euphotic zone via vertical mixing during spring, thereby enhancing CO2 uptake through primary production. Radiocarbon (∆14C) in dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) of seawater has been widely used as a tracer of mixing. However, the DIC-∆14C signature of STMW has yet to be directly measured. We report the DIC-∆14C in twenty seawater samples collected from two stations in the western NP in May 2025 and combine our results with BGC-Argo profiles to observe mixing dynamics within STMW and elucidate its structure. DIC-∆14C values ranged from -49.7–20.5‰ between 10–700 m and varied within the STMW layer (15.5 ± 3.5‰) despite consistent physical properties. The STMW core – defined by a minimum potential vorticity (PV) of < 1 (10-10 s-1 m-1) – was located between 230–360 m. Positive DIC-∆14C anomalies (> 20‰) were observed in the lower STMW layer (~400 m) at both stations. Similarly, BGC-Argo profiles of nitrate, pH, and dissolved oxygen diverged below 360 m at station C1. This suggests that while STMW appears physically homogeneous, it may vary biogeochemically. The DIC-∆14C values combined with BGC-Argo profiles show an older STMW mass lies beneath the younger core, indicating that the lower STMW layer may be from the preceding winter. This is consistent with the reported decline of DIC-∆14C concentrations in nearby surface waters in recent years. The heterogeneous distribution of DIC-∆14C within STMW may also indicate vertical mixing, implying that nutrients from the subsurface may be injected into the euphotic zone during spring. This study shows that DIC-∆14C is a sensitive tracer that can be used to detect seasonal layering and heterogeneity within STMW.

presentations.session_title: Multiscale Variabilities in the Western Pacific Ocean and Their Impacts on Multi-disciplinary Aspects
presentations.convener: Akira NAGANO (Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology) nagano@jamstec.go.jp
presentations.session_chairs: Hanna NA (Seoul National University) , Linlin ZHANG (Institute of Oceanology, Chinese Academy of Sciences)
presentations.presentation_title: Linking Noctiluca Scintillans Population Dynamics in Yatsushiro Bay to Potential Long-distance Connectivity Via the SCS and Kuroshio
presentations.abstract: Noctiluca scintillans is a globally distributed harmful algal bloom (HAB) species capable of causing ecological impacts and economic losses to fisheries. Because N. scintillans accumulates near the sea surface, its population dynamics may be strongly influenced by ocean circulation; however, direct evidence linking long-distance transport to local bloom dynamics remains limited. Here, we integrate year-round field observations, single-cell genetic analysis, morphology, and Lagrangian particle-tracking simulations to investigate population connectivity of N. scintillans in Yatsushiro Bay (Kumamoto, Japan). Monthly monitoring revealed two distinct annual abundance peaks: a spring–early summer peak dominated by a Japan–China haplotype (K1) with larger cell sizes, and an autumn peak dominated by an Indonesian (Jakarta-type, K2) haplotype characterized by smaller cells comparable to Jakarta populations. This seasonal genetic and morphological turnover suggests contributions from both regional and non-local populations within a single annual cycle. To assess whether large-scale ocean circulation could plausibly connect these distant regions, we conducted forward and backward Lagrangian particle-tracking simulations using OSCAR near-surface currents over a 600-day period. Simulations showed low-probability but physically plausible surface connectivity between Indonesian waters and Japan, with all particles reaching Japanese coastal regions consistently transiting through the South China Sea and Kuroshio system. Sensitivity tests across multiple release regions and particle numbers produced similar pathway structures, although arrivals remained rare. Taken together, our results indicate that N. scintillans populations in Yatsushiro Bay likely reflect a combination of local persistence and episodic long-distance contributions. These findings highlight how rare advective events under specific circulation states may influence plankton biogeography and HAB dynamics in a changing climate.

presentations.session_title: Multiscale Variabilities in the Western Pacific Ocean and Their Impacts on Multi-disciplinary Aspects
presentations.convener: Akira NAGANO (Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology) nagano@jamstec.go.jp
presentations.session_chairs: Hanna NA (Seoul National University) , Linlin ZHANG (Institute of Oceanology, Chinese Academy of Sciences)
presentations.presentation_title: Integrated Dynamics Of The Western Pacific Margin: Kuroshio Submesoscale Processes, Subduction, And Deep-Sea Ecosystems
presentations.institution: Taiwan Ocean Research Institute, National Institutes of Applied Research
presentations.abstract: The western Pacific margin off eastern Taiwan is a key region where the Kuroshio Current, interacts with active subduction zones and complex bathymetry, shaping ocean circulation, biogeochemical processes, and marine ecosystems. Interactions among physical, geological, and ecological processes occur across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales, yet remain poorly constrained due to limited integrated observations, particularly in the deep ocean. To address this gap, the West Pacific International Observation and Research Station will be established by the Taiwan Ocean Research Institute, NIAR. This presentation will outline key research themes developed under this framework, with an emphasis on Kuroshio dynamics and their broader Earth system impacts. The first theme will focus on the submesoscale dynamics of the Kuroshio, combining SWOT wide-swath satellite altimetry with in situ observations to examine momentum balance regimes in high-Rossby-number flows. By resolving submesoscale eddies and frontal structures, this work will quantify their roles in vertical exchange, energy dissipation, and biogeochemical modulation along the Kuroshio. The second theme will examine how subduction-related tectonic structures and steep bathymetry along the southern Ryukyu margin influence Kuroshio pathways, mesoscale variability, and associated geohazards. Integrated long-offset multi-channel seismic, ocean-bottom seismometers, and gravity observations will be used to refine crustal velocity models and improve constraints on earthquake and tsunami risks affecting the western Pacific margin. The third theme will address deep-sea benthic ecosystems and pelagic–benthic coupling in eastern Taiwan, a globally significant biodiversity hotspot. Non-destructive surveys integrating multibeam bathymetry, optical imaging, ROV observations, and eDNA will be applied to assess how Kuroshio variability and topography-induced upwelling regulate deep-sea habitat distribution and ecosystem connectivity. Together, these themes will highlight the western Pacific margin as a tightly coupled ocean–Earth system. This integrated approach will advance understanding of Kuroshio-driven impacts while strengthening international collaboration and sustained observation capacity in the region.

presentations.session_title: Oceanic Big Data and Artificial Intelligence Oceanography
presentations.convener: Guangjun XU (Guangdong Ocean University) gjxu_gdou@yeah.net
presentations.session_chairs: Guoqi HAN (Fisheries and Oceans Canada)
presentations.presentation_title: Long-term Variability of Sea Surface and Vertical Ocean Structure in the Southern Indo-Pacific under Climate Warming
presentations.abstract: Global warming has intensified oceanic heat absorption, resulting in alterations not only at the sea surface but also within the vertical structure of oceans. The southern Indonesian seas, situated in the Indo-Pacific region, sustain seasonally driven coastal upwelling systems that are crucial for marine productivity; however, their long-term vertical responses to climate warming remain poorly understood. This study investigated the impact of long-term ocean warming on the vertical ocean structure and upwelling variability in southern Indonesian waters from 1993 to 2023. Using oceanic reanalysis datasets, long-term trends in sea surface temperature (SST), ocean heat content (OHC), mixed layer depth (MLD), thermocline depth (D20), and sea surface height (SSH) were analyzed, focusing on the boreal summer season (JJA). The results showed a significant increase in ocean heat content, with stronger warming during JJA, indicating enhanced subsurface heat accumulation. Concurrent changes in MLD and D20 reveal thermocline deepening and strengthened vertical stratification, leading to increased upper-ocean stability. Variability in the upwelling characteristics was further examined using the Topographic Position Index (TPI). The results indicate a reduction and delayed onset of upwelling during the late period (2014–2023) compared to the early period (1993–2002), along with a shift toward more frequent surface warming responses, particularly in the eastern part of the study area. These changes are closely associated with oceanic processes, such as the Indonesian Throughflow, South Java Current, and coastal Kelvin wave activity, which modulate thermocline displacement. Long-term ocean warming alters the vertical structure of the upper ocean by deepening the thermocline and enhancing stratification, thereby weakening coastal upwelling. Such changes may reduce the nutrient supply to the euphotic zone and pose potential risks to marine productivity.

presentations.session_chairs: Guoqi HAN (Fisheries and Oceans Canada)
presentations.presentation_title: Sea Ice Reduction in the Barents–kara Sea Enhances June Precipitation in the Yangtze River Basin
presentations.abstract: This study investigates the influence of June sea surface temperature (SST) and sea ice in the Barents–Kara Sea (BKS) on concurrent rainfall variability in the Yangtze River basin from 1982 to 2021 using both observational data and numerical experiments. The observed decrease in BKS sea ice and the corresponding increase in SST during June aligns with enhanced precipitation in the Yangtze River basin on an interannual timescale. The BKS thermal forcing induces an equivalent barotropic Rossby wave train in the middle and upper troposphere, which propagates southeastward to the Northwest Pacific (NWP). This Rossby wave train features two positive centers over the BKS and NWP and one negative center above Baikal Lake. The strengthened NWP subtropical high and upper-level westerly jet contribute to increased rainfall in the Yangtze River basin by enhancing moisture transport and anomalous ascending motions. These findings provide important implications for predicting summer rainfall in East Asia.

presentations.convener: Guangjun XU (Guangdong Ocean University) gjxu_gdou@yeah.net
presentations.session_chairs: Guoqi HAN (Fisheries and Oceans Canada)
presentations.presentation_title: Contrasting Multiscale Mechanisms of Extreme Rainfall Events in Henan Province: the July 2021 and September 2024 Cases
presentations.abstract: Two catastrophic rainfall events struck Henan Province, China, on 20 July 2021 and 18 September 2024, producing record-breaking 24-hour precipitation totals of 624.1 mm in Zhengzhou and 272.6 mm in Xiayi, respectively. Despite being initiated under a remarkably similar synoptic-scale backdrop characterized by dual typhoons and an anomalous Western Pacific Subtropical High (WPSH), the two events diverged dramatically in their evolution, intensity, and spatial distribution. This study investigates the multiscale processes responsible for this divergence using surface observations and ERA5 reanalysis data. We identify two critical divergence points. First, moisture transport pathways differed markedly: the 2021 Zhengzhou event drew moisture from both the northwestern Pacific and the South China Sea through a dual-channel setup, whereas the 2024 Xiayi event relied on a single dominant corridor originating from the northwestern Pacific, steered by the landfalling Typhoon Bebinca. Second, the triggering and organization of the mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) were governed by distinct mechanisms—the synergistic coupling of a Huang-Huai vortex (HHV), low-level jets (LLJs), and orographic lifting along the Taihang Mountains in 2021 versus cold-air-induced frontogenesis during Bebinca's extratropical transition in 2024. These findings highlight how subtle differences at finer scales can lead to vastly different extreme outcomes under seemingly identical large-scale conditions, offering crucial insights for improving regional forecasting.

presentations.convener: Guangjun XU (Guangdong Ocean University) gjxu_gdou@yeah.net
presentations.session_chairs: Guoqi HAN (Fisheries and Oceans Canada)
presentations.presentation_title: AI-Driven Global Sea Surface Salinity Retrieval from Ocean Color
presentations.institution: Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Sea surface salinity (SSS) is a key variable for understanding ocean circulation, freshwater fluxes, and climate variability. Despite its importance, reliable monitoring remains challenging, particularly in coastal and low salinity regions where variability is strong. L-band satellite missions such as Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) provide global SSS observations but are constrained near the coast by coarse spatial resolution and land-related signal interference. While ocean color remote sensing offers superior spatial and temporal resolution, existing SSS retrieval methods have largely been developed as region dependent algorithms, and a globally applicable ocean color-based retrieval framework remains absent. This study proposes a global high resolution SSS retrieval framework that integrates ocean color observations with a two-step training strategy, using satellite derived and in situ SSS measurements as reference data to construct a sufficiently large and diverse training dataset. Our results demonstrated that global AI models outperformed conventional region-specific algorithms, providing improved accuracy in coastal domains. Evaluation against in situ measurements showed that the proposed model achieves higher performance (R² = 0.85; RMSE = 0.74 psu) than SMAP (R² = 0.80; RMSE = 0.82 psu). Comparisons with numerical models and level 4 satellite SSS products further show that the resulting high resolution SSS fields more effectively capture fine scale variability in coastal regions. This study demonstrates the feasibility of a globally applicable ocean color-based SSS retrieval framework, showing that data driven approaches can achieve consistent performance across regions and improved representation of coastal and low salinity variability compared to existing satellite observations and numerical models.

presentations.session_title: Oceanic Big Data and Artificial Intelligence Oceanography
presentations.convener: Guangjun XU (Guangdong Ocean University) gjxu_gdou@yeah.net
presentations.session_chairs: Guoqi HAN (Fisheries and Oceans Canada)
presentations.presentation_title: Cloud-free Sea Surface Temperature Reconstruction from Multi-satellite Observations by Deep Learning
presentations.abstract: Sea surface temperature (SST) is a key variable for understanding air-sea interactions, yet resolving submesoscale processes requires SST fields that are both super-resolution (SR) and spatially complete. Infrared radiometers, such as the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS), provide SR capability but suffer from severe cloud contamination. Conversely, microwave sensors, such as the Advanced Microwave Scanning Radiometer 2 (AMSR2), offer all-weather global coverage but at a low-resolution (LR) that lacks the spatial detail needed to capture small-scale features. To address these information loss issues, we introduced the Remote Sensing Cross-scale Reconstruction (RSCR) deep learning (DL) network, which jointly recovered spatial resolution and swath coverage by leveraging the unique multi-scale nature of remote sensing data, namely incomplete SR VIIRS and all-weather LR AMSR2. RSCR employed (1) temporal context through 7-day sequences to guide reconstruction and (2) spatial complementarity, using cloud-free infrared observations to supply fine-scale texture while using gap-free LR microwave fields to provide the large-scale background guidance. The architecture of RSCR consisted of two encoders: a multi-level ConvLSTM encoder capturing temporal evolution and integrating spatial features across scales, and a difference-extraction encoder capturing spatial structures from spatiotemporal differences. Features from both encoders are fused via an attention to combine long-term dynamics with short-term variations, followed by a multi-modal decoder for cross-modal interaction. Experiments evaluated RSCR in terms of accuracy and feature resolution. Evaluation on the validation dataset showed that RSCR achieved an RMSE of 0.32 °C, a 30.4% reduction relative to the current operational baseline, the Multi-scale Ultra-high Resolution (MUR) L4 product. Power spectral density (PSD) analysis showed that RSCR better preserved submesoscale energy and features than MUR. In a typhoon case study, RSCR reconstructed cold wakes with peak cooling of −5.91 °C, about 20.4% stronger than MUR (−4.91 °C), suggesting that typhoon-induced cooling may be underestimated in conventional SST products.

presentations.convener: Guangjun XU (Guangdong Ocean University) gjxu_gdou@yeah.net
presentations.session_chairs: Guoqi HAN (Fisheries and Oceans Canada)
presentations.presentation_title: Pattern Analysis and Machine Learning of Chesapeake Bay Plume Dynamics
presentations.abstract: We examined the spatiotemporal dynamics of estuarine plumes in Chesapeake Bay using long-term numerical simulations. Empirical Orthogonal Function and Self-Organizing Map analyses revealed six dominant plume patterns, primarily controlled by freshwater discharge, wind forcing, and surface elevation. Seasonal plume expansion was largely governed by freshwater discharge, while upwelling- and downwelling-favorable winds exerted secondary but significant influences. To predict daily plume variability, we developed a hybrid machine learning model that combines a Convolutional Neural Network with transformer architecture and an attention mechanism. Driven by physically informed parameter transformations representing freshwater discharge, tidal elevation, shelf salinity, and wind forcing, the model achieved a mean and maximum root-mean-square errors of 0.8 and 1.73, respectively, demonstrating the value of embedding physical processes into machine learning feature design.We further evaluated the sensitivity of model performance to input feature selection and discussed key challenges in applying machine learning to estuarine plume diagnostics under variable external forcings. These findings provide a foundation for data-driven forecasting and improved understanding of estuarine plume dynamics under changing environmental conditions.

presentations.convener: Guangjun XU (Guangdong Ocean University) gjxu_gdou@yeah.net
presentations.session_chairs: Guoqi HAN (Fisheries and Oceans Canada)
presentations.presentation_title: Regional Differences in Satellite-based Nutrient Estimation Between the Inner and Outer Seto Inland Sea Using Machine Learning
presentations.abstract: Accurate and spatially continuous nutrient fields are critical for understanding coastal biogeochemical dynamics and supporting ecosystem and biogeochemical modeling. However, satellite-based nutrient estimation remains particularly challenging in optically complex coastal environments. This study investigates regional differences in satellite-derived nutrient estimation between the inner and outer Seto Inland Sea (SIS) using a Gradient Boosted Regression Trees (GBRT) machine learning framework over the period 2013–2021. MODIS Level-2 observations of sea surface temperature and chlorophyll-a were reconstructed using the Data-Interpolating Empirical Orthogonal Functions Plus (DINEOF+) method to enhance spatial and temporal continuity. These reconstructed variables served as predictors in GBRT models to estimate key biogeochemical parameters, including dissolved inorganic carbon, dissolved oxygen, phosphate, nitrate, silicate, and pH. Model training and validation were conducted using in situ observations compiled from multiple authoritative sources, including the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA), the World Ocean Database (WOD), the Japan Oceanographic Data Center (JODC), and the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism (MLIT), Japan. Model performance was evaluated separately for the inner and outer SIS. The GBRT results consistently demonstrate higher estimation accuracy in the outer SIS, characterized by higher coefficients of determination and lower error metrics, compared to the inner region. The reduced performance in the inner SIS is attributed to increased optical complexity associated with elevated turbidity, strong riverine inputs, and intensified anthropogenic influences. In contrast, the more stable optical and hydrographic conditions of the outer SIS facilitate more reliable satellite-based nutrient estimation.These findings potentially underscore the robustness of the GBRT approach in relatively less complex coastal waters and highlight the potential of satellite-based GBRT-derived nutrient products to provide reliable boundary conditions for coastal and regional biogeochemical modeling in the SIS.

presentations.session_title: Dynamics Driven Biogeochemical Cycle in Coastal Oceans
presentations.convener: Yuntao WANG (Second Institute of Oceanography, Ministry of Natural Resources) yuntao.wang@sio.org.cn
presentations.session_chairs: Xinyu GUO (Ehime University) , Zongpei JIANG (Zhejiang University)
presentations.presentation_title: POC Lateral Transport and Differential Burial in the Pacific Arctic Region
presentations.abstract: Investigating the burial and release of organic carbon (OC) in marine sediments is essential for elucidating the source-to-sink characteristics of Arctic carbon during climate transitions and its driving role in global change. Combining modern observations of suspended particulate matter (SPM) and ice algae with sedimentary OC isotope records, we analysed the transport, burial, and degradation mechanisms of organic carbon from different sources in the Pacific Arctic Region since the Late Pleistocene. The results indicate that hydrodynamic sorting of terrestrial and marine OC in the upper water column is the primary factor regulating their spatial distribution, degradation extent, and climate feedback. The easily suspended terrestrial OC is mainly concentrated in surface waters and undergoes long-distance lateral transport with ocean currents, suffering intense degradation in the water column and uppermost sediments. In contrast, marine OC, represented by Melosira arctica, is characterized by rapid settling; it detaches from sea ice primarily before August and contributes approximately 55% to the carbon burial in deep basins. This fraction of OC is preferentially buried in submarine canyons and shelf edges, undergoing sustainable degradation, which effectively enhances the Arctic carbon sink capacity on a millennial timescale. This study reveals a potential negative feedback mechanism of the Arctic carbon sink in the context of warming, which is crucial for assessing the Arctic's regulatory capacity in the global carbon cycle and climate change.

presentations.convener: Yuntao WANG (Second Institute of Oceanography, Ministry of Natural Resources) yuntao.wang@sio.org.cn
presentations.session_chairs: Xinyu GUO (Ehime University) , Zongpei JIANG (Zhejiang University)
presentations.presentation_title: Short-term Impacts of Typhoon Events on Upwelling System and Carbon Dynamics in Coastal Water
presentations.abstract: Upwelling systems play a critical role in regulating the coastal ocean carbon cycle by modulating air-sea CO₂ exchange through coupled physical-biological processes. This study investigates the characteristics of an upwelling system and its short-term biogeochemical responses before and after a typhoon event, based on multidisciplinary observations conducted offshore of eastern Hainan Island in the summer of 2023. Using a two end-member mixing model, the relative contributions of temperature, mixing, and biological processes to pCO₂ changes were quantified to reveal the coupled mechanism of typhoon–upwelling–carbon cycle. Results show that the typhoon significantly altered the hydrographic structure and pCO₂ distribution in the upwelling zone. During the intensifying phase, strong wind stress enhanced the upwelling of deep, high-CO₂ water, with physical mixing dominating and causing a sharp increase in surface pCO₂, turning the area into a notable CO₂ source. In the weakening phase, reduced winds and sustained high nutrient levels promoted phytoplankton photosynthesis, strengthening the biological drawdown effect on pCO₂. The results indicated that physical processes dominated overall (50%–60%), while biological contributions increased notably later (30%–40%), reflecting a typical “physics-dominated, biology-buffered” pCO₂ regulatory mechanism in the Qiongdong upwelling during typhoon events. The typhoon enhanced short-term CO₂ release to the atmosphere, whereas biological uptake partially offset carbon fluxes post-event, driving the system toward a new dynamic balance.

presentations.session_title: Dynamics Driven Biogeochemical Cycle in Coastal Oceans
presentations.convener: Yuntao WANG (Second Institute of Oceanography, Ministry of Natural Resources) yuntao.wang@sio.org.cn
presentations.session_chairs: Xinyu GUO (Ehime University) , Zongpei JIANG (Zhejiang University)
presentations.presentation_title: Impacts of Multiple Nutrient Sources on the Nitrogen Inventory and Budget of a Semi-enclosed Coastal Sea
presentations.abstract: Semi-enclosed coastal seas act as transitional zones between terrestrial areas and open ocean. The active biogeochemical processes there play a crucial role in global material cycles. Nutrients from diverse sources collectively shape the nitrogen inventory and budget in the coastal oceans through the combined influence of physical dynamics and biogeochemical processes. In this study, we assess the relative contributions of different nutrient sources to the ecosystem of the Seto Inland Sea, a semi-enclosed sea in Japan. Using a three-dimensional coupled hydrodynamic–biogeochemical model with an embedded tracking technique, we show that the open ocean accounts for 61 % and 46 % to the inventories of dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN) and phytoplankton, respectively. The conversion of DIN into particulate organic nitrogen (PON) was also mainly driven by nitrogen from the open ocean, except during the summer. Riverine nitrogen primarily supported the deposition of PON to the seafloor, whereas the nitrogen from the open ocean dominated the PON flux exported to the open ocean. These results establish a baseline framework for the future assessments of coastal responses to global changes.

presentations.session_title: Dynamics Driven Biogeochemical Cycle in Coastal Oceans
presentations.convener: Yuntao WANG (Second Institute of Oceanography, Ministry of Natural Resources) yuntao.wang@sio.org.cn
presentations.session_chairs: Xinyu GUO (Ehime University) , Zongpei JIANG (Zhejiang University)
presentations.presentation_title: Simulation of Red Tide Distribution in the Seto Inland Sea Using a High-resolution SCHISM–COSINE Model, validated with Satellite Observations.
presentations.abstract: The Seto Inland Sea (SIS) is a semi-enclosed coastal region in Japan adjacent to highly urbanized areas such as Osaka Bay and Hiroshima Bay. During the 1970s, more than 200 red tide events per year were reported in the SIS, mainly due to untreated domestic and industrial wastewater. Following the introduction of advanced wastewater treatment technologies, the frequency of red tide occurrences has decreased to approximately 70–80 events annually in recent years.In this study, a red tide event that occurred in July 2021 in the southern waters of Miyajima, Hiroshima, was simulated using a coupled high-resolution numerical modeling system and validated using satellite-derived images. The hydrodynamic ocean circulation model SCHISM, previously validated in the SIS for tidal elevation, currents, temperature, and salinity, was employed to provide physical conditions for the biogeochemical model COSINE. COSINE simulates plankton growth and mortality based on nutrient concentrations and seawater properties.The model successfully reproduced the spatial distribution and temporal evolution of the red tide, showing good agreement with satellite-observed surface chlorophyll-a patterns. Results indicate that nutrient inputs discharged from the Ota River, the primary freshwater and nutrient source to Hiroshima Bay, played a dominant role in initiating and sustaining the red tide within the inner bay. The high-resolution configuration of SCHISM enabled detailed representation of river plume dynamics and coastal circulation, which were essential for resolving the observed red tide distribution.These results demonstrate the effectiveness of coupling high-resolution hydrodynamic and biogeochemical models with satellite observations for understanding red tide dynamics and provide a useful framework for coastal water quality assessment and management in the Seto Inland Sea. In addition, air–sea CO₂ fluxes were calculated and analyzed to assess the role of the SIS as a blue carbon storage system.

presentations.presentation_title: Seasonal Predictability of Tropical Cyclone Frequency and an Indicator of Mass Coral Bleaching in the Western North Pacific
presentations.institution: Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: In this study, we examined the seasonal predictability of tropical cyclone (TC) frequency and Degree Heating Weeks (DHWs). DHWs are a widely used indicator of coral thermal stress and a strong predictor of coral bleaching. We used a 108-member seasonal reforecast from 1982 to 2022 for our analysis. Our findings revealed that the model accurately predicts summer TC frequency and DHWs around Okinawa and Taiwan. Additionally, we found that the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) significantly impacts TC frequency prediction in the region. Suppressing TC activity increased DHW by weakening cooling via vertical diffusion. Successful predictions could help reduce the risk of coral reef collapse by facilitating the implementation of necessary adaptation measures.

presentations.presentation_title: Extratropical Forcing of Enso in an Extratropical SST Pacemaker Experiment
presentations.institution: School of Science, the University of Tokyo
presentations.abstract: While El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) arises from the tropical ocean-atmosphere coupled dynamics, extratropical climate variability has been proposed to precondition and excite ENSO through a range of pathways. One prominent example is the seasonal footprinting mechanism (SFM), in which the Pacific Meridional Mode (PMM; NPMM/SPMM) persists and subsequently influences the equatorial Pacific. However, it remains unclear to what extent extratropical SST variability explains ENSO variance and how such forcing modifies ENSO characteristics, including its preferred timescales and persistence. Here we evaluate the contribution of extratropical SST variability to ENSO using a set of GFDL-CM2.1 experiments. We compare a fully coupled pre-industrial (1860) control simulation with an SST pacemaker ensemble (XTOGA; 20 members) in which extratropical SSTs are restored toward a 200-year segment of the control simulation, whose ensemble mean thus isolates the tropical response to extratropical SST variability. The XTOGA ensemble mean Niño3.4 index significantly correlates with the control Niño3.4, peaking in boreal winter (NDJ; r=0.54) and explaining ~29% of its winter interannual variance. Boreal spring NPMM and SPMM indices lead the winter Nino3.4 (r=0.35 and 0.39, respectively), indicating distinct subtropical precursors. Composite analyses show that positive NPMM and SPMM events lead El Niño–like conditions: subtropical warming enhances precipitation and induces a westward-extending low-pressure response, and the associated westerly anomalies weaken the trades and reduce evaporative cooling, amplifying SST anomalies, which is consistent with WES feedback, as part of the SFM. Extratropically forced ENSO is more persistent than tropical internally-driven variability, likely due to more persistent NPMM and SPMM. We also find evidence of a teleconnection from western equatorial Pacific SST anomalies that strengthens the Aleutian Low and generates wind anomalies favorable for NPMM growth, suggesting a coupled tropical–extratropical feedback that can help sustain multi-year ENSO anomalies.

presentations.presentation_title: Global and Regional Changes in Cumulative Energy of Extreme Coastal Wave Storm Events
presentations.abstract: Understanding how extreme coastal wave storm events have changed over time is essential for assessing coastal hazards and shoreline erosion. While previous global studies have largely focused on trends in wave height, changes in cumulative wave energy of extreme coastal wave storm events have not yet been assessed. Cumulative wave energy, which integrates wave height and event duration, has been found to be a reliable indicator of coastal erosion potential, particularly along wave-dominated sandy coastlines.This study presents a global, event-based assessment of long-term changes in cumulative wave energy of extreme coastal wave storm events using ERA5 wave data. Coastal wave storm events are identified using a Peaks-Over-Threshold approach, and cumulative wave energy is computed as the time-integrated squared significant wave height over each event. At each coastal location, the median (Q50) cumulative wave energy of the most energetic events (Top 10 and Top 50) is compared between two periods (1979–2001 and 2002–2024). Corresponding changes in event duration and peak wave height are also analysed, and results are aggregated across IPCC coastal regions to assess regional-scale patterns. Results indicate an overall global increase in cumulative wave energy of extreme coastal wave storm events, accompanied by pronounced regional variability. Larger increases are generally observed across Southern Hemisphere coastlines, particularly western Africa, while weaker or negative changes are evident in parts of Europe. Changes in cumulative wave energy are more strongly associated with changes in event duration than with changes in peak wave height. This analysis provides key insights into regional hotspots related to shoreline erosion associated with individual wave storm events and highlights that coastal wave storm energy of the most extreme events has increased in some regions over recent decades.

presentations.presentation_title: Influence of Internal North Atlantic Variability on Mid-latitude North Pacific Warming
presentations.institution: Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: The mid-latitude North Pacific has remained anomalously warm over the past several years. This prolonged warming is closely associated with severe marine heatwaves and has contributed to summer heatwaves in East Asia. While many studies have emphasized local air-sea interactions and teleconnections from the tropical Pacific, the influence of the North Atlantic on North Pacific variability has not been fully assessed. Here we show that internal sea surface temperature (SST) variability in the mid-latitude North Atlantic explains 16% of internal SST variability in the Kuroshio region in idealized climate model simulations. Specifically, positive SST anomalies in the Gulf Stream region weaken the Aleutian Low over the North Pacific and trigger oceanic Rossby waves. The associated northward shift of the Kuroshio Extension enhances northward warm water transport, leading to positive SST anomalies over the mid-latitude North Pacific. This mechanism is further supported by sensitivity experiments in which North Atlantic SST anomalies are restored toward the observed SST anomalies. Furthermore, climate models with higher oceanic spatial resolution reproduce the proposed mechanism better than coarser-resolution models. This result implies that high-resolution ocean modeling is critical for the predictability of mid-latitude North Pacific climate variability, especially for prolonged warming and extreme marine heatwaves.

presentations.presentation_title: Strengthening Influence of Enso on the Equatorial Atlantic and Its Implications for Predictability
presentations.institution: Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) affects weather and climate around the world but its impact on the equatorial Atlantic has been surprisingly inconsistent, with some major El Niño events followed by cooling in the equatorial Atlantic, while others were followed by warming. Here we use climate change projections from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) to examine how ENSO’s relation with the equatorial Atlantic may change under global warming. Similar to ENSO, variability in the equatorial Atlantic, also known as the Atlantic Zonal Mode (AZM), is influenced by the Bjerknes feedback, in which sea-surface temperature (SST) anomalies drive deep convection and a surface wind response that amplifies the original SST anomalies. Due to the stabilization of the atmosphere under global warming, this Atlantic feedback weakens in the CMIP6 projections. Instead, many models suggest a scenario in which the AZM is dominantly driven by ENSO’s thermodynamic forcing, namely the tropics-wide tropospheric warming (cooling) that follows El Niño (La Niña) events. As a result, ocean dynamics and coupled air-sea feedbacks play a much weaker role, while ENSO’s influence on the AZM becomes more consistent. Analysis with a simple linear prediction scheme suggests that this can also increase the predictability of the AZM, due to the high predictability of ENSO. While many models envision an ENSO-dominated future, some continue to simulate an independent, dynamically driven AZM until the end of the 21st century. The potential reasons for this disparate behavior will be discussed.

presentations.presentation_title: Seasonal to Interannual Controls on Extreme Events: Roles of Monsoon Dynamics and Vegetation Feedbacks
presentations.institution: Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Extreme weather and climate events are often treated as largely stochastic outcomes of internal atmospheric variability, yet growing evidence indicates that their frequency, intensity, and spatial organization are strongly regulated by processes operating on seasonal to interannual timescales. This talk synthesizes recent advances showing how monsoon dynamics and vegetation–land surface feedbacks provide key sources of memory and predictability for extreme event activity.We highlight how large-scale monsoon circulation variability modulates moisture transport, vertical stability, and convective organization, preconditioning regions for heatwaves, droughts, floods, and compound extremes. Superimposed on these dynamical controls, vegetation and soil-moisture states introduce additional persistence through evapotranspiration, surface roughness, and radiative feedbacks, effectively amplifying or damping extreme responses. Observational analyses and simplified diagnostics reveal that vegetation anomalies—whether driven by antecedent climate variability or human land management—can shift monsoon rainfall distributions and alter the likelihood of extremes well beyond synoptic timescales.By framing extremes as emergent outcomes of coupled atmosphere–land–biosphere interactions, rather than purely weather-scale phenomena, we identify predictable windows of extreme event activity tied to monsoon phase, land-surface memory, and their nonlinear coupling. The implications for seasonal forecasting, risk assessment, and climate adaptation are discussed, emphasizing the need to better represent vegetation dynamics and land–atmosphere coupling in prediction systems to improve forecasts of extremes in a warming, human-modified climate.

presentations.presentation_title: Modulation Of Mesoscale Convective Complexes (MCC) By The Quasi-biennial Oscillation (QBO) And Equatorial Kelvin Waves Over The Indonesian Maritime Continent (1991–2020)
presentations.abstract: The Indonesian Maritime Continent (IMC) is a key region for global atmospheric circulation, yet the long-term influence of stratospheric variability on organized convection and mesoscale convective complexes (MCCs) remains unclear. We examine relationships between the stratospheric Quasi Biennial Oscillation (QBO), equatorial Kelvin wave activity, and convection over the IMC during 1991–2020. Zonal wind from the JRA 3Q reanalysis across 10–100 hPa is used to characterize QBO phases and their vertical evolution. QBO phase is defined by the sign of the equatorial zonal mean wind at 50 hPa (u50), separating westerly months (u50 > 0) and easterly months (u50 < 0). Kelvin wave activity is represented by equatorial (5°S–5°N) zonal wind anomalies as an indicator of intraseasonal equatorial disturbances that may condition convection under different background states. As an initial proxy for deep convection relevant to environments that favor MCC development, we use NOAA daily outgoing longwave radiation (OLR) averaged over the IMC domain (10°S–10°N, 90°E–150°E). OLR is converted to monthly means and composited by QBO phase, including 190 westerly and 170 easterly months. Preliminary composites show slightly lower IMC mean OLR during QBO easterly months than during QBO westerly months (222.10 and 223.25 W m⁻², respectively), consistent with marginally stronger deep convection during the easterly phase in a domain mean sense. Ongoing work will implement MCC identification based on individual events, quantify statistical robustness using resampling or permutation tests, and examine spatial and seasonal structure across the IMC. These steps will test whether QBO phase and Kelvin wave activity are associated with systematic changes in MCC frequency and characteristics.
