presentations.session_chairs: Hajoon SONG (Yonsei University) , Shinichiro KIDA (Kyushu University) , Xinru LI (Tohoku University)
presentations.presentation_title: Beyond Lethal Temperatures: Factors Behind the Disappearance of Chum Salmon from Their Southern Margins Under Climate Change
presentations.institution: Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: The Tone River in Japan represents one of the southern limit of the distributions of chum salmon (Oncorhynchus keta) on the western side of the North Pacific, but the number of adult chum salmon observed here has declined dramatically since 2013 and reached zero in 2024. The factors behind the recent decline of the chum salmon population in the Tone River were investigated by using ocean reanalysis data and a 20-year particle-tracking simulation. Virtual chum salmon fry were released at the mouth of the Tone River in spring each year with six different swimming strategies to evaluate the effects of ocean currents on the population growth rate of salmon. None of the simulated scenarios reproduced the recent decline in the population regardless of the swimming strategy and addition of lethal temperature thresholds. Instead, the decline in population growth rate appears to be correlated with warming water temperature and reduced zooplankton abundance caused by the northward shifts of the Kuroshio/Kuroshio Extension and Oyashio. Along the coast of northeastern Japan, the warm, nutrient-poor Kuroshio/Kuroshio Extension replaced the cold, nutrient-rich Oyashio on the migration route of chum salmon fry, increasing the water temperature and reducing zooplankton abundance. Partial correlation analysis of the water temperature and zooplankton abundance indicated that the latter was the main influencing factor coherently related to the population growth rate of salmon. The reduced zooplankton abundance would affect the growth and survival of chum salmon fry, which would result in a decline in population growth. The northward shift of the Kuroshio/Kuroshio Extension and Oyashio may continue or return southward depending on the effects of climate change, which will greatly influence the future population growth of chum salmon and whether they come back to the Tone River.

presentations.presentation_title: Assessment of Various Marine Carbon Dioxide Removal (mcdr) Strategies in the Northern Indian Ocean
presentations.abstract: Carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere have drastically increased in the last two centuries. Cuts in its emission and getting rid of the excess CO2 in the atmosphere is the priority of this decade to lessen the harmful effects of climate change. Technological strategies are key to the sequestration of CO2 from the atmosphere. The oceans substantially contribute towards slowing the increase in atmospheric CO2. However, we need to enhance the oceanic CO2 sink capacity by using different Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR) techniques. Mesocosm experiments conducted in the eastern Arabian Sea have looked at Ocean fertilization (using Natural Buoyant Flakes, Rice husk and Bamboo), and Sargassum. Our work shows that Sargassum has the largest CO2 drawdown capacity. However, the above techniques can have negative consequences for which we need to reconfigure the strategies to avoid environmental alterations. Our results indicate that nutrient delivery mechanism, control over micrograzers and getting rid of the excess organic matter are important factors that need to be tackled for better CDR.

presentations.convener: Hajoon SONG (Yonsei University) hajsong@yonsei.ac.kr

presentations.presentation_title: Asymmetric Responses of the Climate System and Carbon Cycle to CO2 Forcing
presentations.abstract: We assess the long‑term stability of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) and its role in climate reversibility using idealized simulations with the Max Planck Institute Earth System Model (MPI‑ESM). In experiments where atmospheric CO₂ is increased to eight times its pre‑industrial value, held constant to equilibrium, and then decreased at the same rate to pre‑industrial levels, the AMOC shows no hysteresis in response to CO₂ forcing or anomalous freshwater input over North Atlantic deep‑water formation regions. Recovery trajectories lie above weakening trajectories, an offset arising from rapid CO₂ change that prevents quasi‑equilibrium. AMOC stability is governed by both anomalous freshwater forcing and intensified tropical evaporation in a warmed climate. Heat and carbon uptake during CO₂ increase differ from their release during CO₂ decrease. A strong AMOC during recovery enhances ocean efficiency in releasing stored heat and carbon, contributing to surface cooling under CO₂ drawdown. While rising CO₂ effects are well studied, the responses of the climate system and carbon cycle to decreasing and negative CO₂ emissions are less understood. Using MPI‑ESM‑LR with an interactive carbon cycle, we run large ensembles to examine changes in atmospheric CO₂ growth and carbon sinks under varying emissions. Negative emissions after ~2100 turn both ocean and land into CO₂ sources. Climate–carbon responses along decreasing pathways are asymmetric relative to increasing pathways, with uncertainty from internal variability. Differences in uptake and release, and in ocean storage of heat and carbon, shape transient responses to cumulative emissions. Combining AMOC stability analysis with carbon–climate asymmetry simulations provides new insight into climate irreversibility and the processes influencing the success of deep emission reductions and negative‑emission strategies in climate mitigation.

presentations.convener: Hajoon SONG (Yonsei University) hajsong@yonsei.ac.kr

presentations.presentation_title: Vertically Resolving Biogeochemical And Physical Parameters Of Sea-Ice Brine
presentations.abstract: From the physical and biogeochemical perspective of sea ice, a unique property is the presence of brine entrapped into pockets in the sea ice during seawater freezing. While individual brine inclusions are often limited to a few millimetres in size, they can amount to as much as 30-40% of the overall sea-ice volume and affect the physical and biogeochemical properties of sea ice. The brine often contains biogeochemically important constituents, like nutrients and algae, concentrated from the seawater during freezing. Importantly, brine inclusions and volumes are far from static. A mix of physical (melting) and chemical (salt depressing the freezing point) drivers allow brine volumes to increase with temperature following the seasonal climate. With high brine inclusion connectivity, brine (and any biogeochemical parameters it carries) can drain out of the ice due to buoyancy or climb up into the snowpack or frost flowers due to capillary action. However, brine is extremely difficult to sample, especially from discrete depths within sea ice. Most studies collect bulk brine from partially drilled core holes or infer values from whole sections of sea ice which may have lost some brine during extraction. Here we propose a new method for collecting a vertical profile of brine samples in order to study the mobility of dissolved and particulate nutrients (macro and micro, e.g., iron) in the brine network of sea ice from Saroma-ko, Japan. We also assess the presence of algae inside the sea ice in the context of nutrient mobility. These findings help us to better link physical (largely temperature) and biogeochemical processes (nutrient fluxes and algal growth) occurring inside sea ice and brine, which can be directly related to the impacts of future warming on the sea-ice system and algal inhabitants.

presentations.presentation_title: Control of Organic Matter Reactivity, Sedimentation Rate and Shelf Geology on Divergent Diagenetic Pathways in Benguela Margin Sediments
presentations.institution: Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: The contrast in pore water chemistry between the steeper Angola Basin shelf characterized by high-sedimentation and low-organic matter content, and the gradual Cape Basin characterized by low-sedimentation and high-organic matter content (ODP Leg 175), presents a natural experiment to test the diagenesis of calcite and organic matter. We aim to quantify the underlying processes of organic matter and calcite reactions in sediment by incorporating multi-component kinetic models, such as sulfate reduction, anaerobic oxidation of methane, and carbonate precipitation/dissolution. After calibration to observed sulphate, calcium, and methane profiles, the model successfully replicates the key contrasts: a shallow Sulfate-Methane transition zone (SMTZ) (~22.55 m) with calcium depletion (precipitation) in Angola sites and a deep SMTZ (~ 30.32 m) with calcium enrichment (dissolution) in Cape sites. The high sulfate-reduction-derived organic matter degradation rate (Rorg ~ 0.36 g C m-2 yr-1) in the shallow SMTZ of the Angola Basin is driven by the rapid burial and high organic matter reactivity, which concentrates anaerobic oxidation of methane and alkalinity production at a sharp front. In contrast, the Cape Basin's deeper SMTZ results from the slower degradation of more refractory organic matter (Rorg ~ 0.22 g C m-2 yr-1) over an extended column (~600 m). The opposing calcium signals are quantitatively explained as a kinetic competition: rapid carbonate precipitation at the sharp Angola SMTZ front versus slow, dissolution-driven carbonate reaction in the organic-rich Cape sequence. This study provides a quantitative, process-based framework that resolves how sedimentation rate and organic matter quality jointly govern diagenetic regimes.

presentations.presentation_title: Ice Melting Process in Water Currents and Surface Waves
presentations.abstract: The melting processes of floating ice in surface waves and currents are studied employing laboratory experiments and a numerical model. The numerical model utilizes the enthalpy method to compute the melt rate of the ice block in steady currents over a wide range of velocities, and validated against the results of laboratory experiments. The findings indicate that melt rates increase linearly with the current velocity, and the frontal melt rate of the ice block is approximately twice that of the rear. The ice’s melt rates in periodic waves are higher than those in steady currents. The convective heat transfer between the ice surface and surrounding water dominates the melting process of flat ice floes, even at very low current velocities. In addition, the vertical velocity of the melt plume is relatively small compared to the current velocity. The unstably stratified flow in the wake region of the ice block enhances the turbulent mixing between the meltwater and ambient water, rapidly dissipating the temperature stratification in the wake flow. The mass change rate and thickness melt rate can be predicted using a bulk parameterization model over a wide range of current velocities.

presentations.presentation_title: On the Information Content of Remote Sensing Data
presentations.abstract: We have examined the information content of the primary remote sensing datasets of physical oceanography – SWOT (SSHa,KaRIn), MODIS/SST, VIIRS/SST – using both traditional techniques (power spectral density, P(k)) and by exploring their latent space representations in standard, unsupervised deep-learning models. In addition, we performed comparable analysis on natural and artificial images (e.g. ImageNet), and SSTa and SSHs outputs from a global ocean circulation model (LLC4320). We find the information content of the satellite data – in real and latent space – is qualitatively similar to the most complex natural images (cats, dogs) and greatly exceeds that contained in ocean model outputs. We first characterize the effects of sensor noise, and demonstrate these contribute to the amplitude of P(k) on the smallest scales but have little effect on the latent space representations. Therefore, we propose that the ocean model insufficiently captures dynamics at scales of ~10km and smaller, but the differences (in SST especially) on scales of ~100km remain unexplained. These results suggest that latent space analysis provides an additional metric for assessing the realism of high-resolution ocean models relative to satellite observations.

presentations.convener: Yusuke UCHIYAMA (Kobe University) uchiyama@harbor.kobe-u.ac.jp
presentations.session_chairs: Changming DONG (Nanjing University of Information Science & Technology) , Sung Yong KIM (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology)
presentations.presentation_title: Three-dimensional Structural Characteristics and Geometric Morphology of Marine Heatwaves in the South China Sea
presentations.institution: Nanjing University of Information Science & Technology
presentations.abstract: Marine heatwaves (MHWs)—defined as prolonged episodes of anomalously elevated ocean temperature—have become more frequent across multiple ocean basins in recent decades, exerting profound and sometimes irreversible impacts on marine ecosystems and the broader ocean environment. The majority of extant studies detect MHWs using sea surface temperature and concentrate on horizontal, two-dimensional attributes; consequently, the vertical structure, internal morphology, and fully three-dimensional evolution of these events remain insufficiently resolved. Leveraging the GLORYS12V1 global ocean reanalysis, this investigation establishes a systematic framework for detecting and statistically characterising three-dimensional marine heatwaves within the South China Sea (SCS). Mean intensity maxima are located at the surface; conversely, duration, spatial coverage, and cumulative intensity are governed by subsurface anomalies whose peaks concentrate between 150 m and 220 m, a vertical distribution that antithetically mirrors surface-centric depictions of MHWs. Inspired by existing taxonomies of mesoscale-eddy vertical structures, we introduce an analogous morphological classification for three-dimensional MHWs that recognises five archetypes—bowl, prism, cone, column, and planar configurations—and thereby provides a standardised nomenclature for comparative analyses. Although planar MHWs record the highest occurrence frequency, cone- and column-shaped events—distinguished by pronounced vertical continuity—disproportionately account for cumulative intensity and volumetric magnitude, evidencing the downward penetration and interior reservoir of anomalous heat. The concurrent presence of disparate morphological structures underscores that three-dimensional MHWs within the SCS occupy distinct vertical development stages and are subject to diverse dynamical controls, thereby precluding a single unifying conceptual model.

presentations.session_chairs: Changming DONG (Nanjing University of Information Science & Technology) , Sung Yong KIM (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology)
presentations.presentation_title: Evaluation of the Impact of Internal Tides on GNSS-A Observations Using the Regional Oceanic Modeling System
presentations.institution: Institute of Industrial Science, University of Tokyo
presentations.abstract: Global Navigation Satellite System – Acoustics combination technique (GNSS-A) seafloor crustal deformation observations are a technique for determining seafloor positions with centimeter-level accuracy through acoustic ranging between seafloor-installed acoustic stations and a surface platform. Japan Coast Guard (JCG) has established an observation network known as SGO-A, which has been accumulating data for future earthquake risk assessments. Analysis of acoustic signal communications in GNSS-A requires estimation of three-dimensional variations in the underwater sound-speed field. Yokota et al. (2025, PEPS) demonstrated that positioning accuracy can be improved by analytically accounting for the period and amplitude of internal tides. They also showed that GNSS-A data simultaneously can serve as secondary observations of internal tides. Therefore, further improvements in GNSS-A accuracy require refinement of modeling approaches and the development of methods to estimate and remove smaller-scale field disturbances, such as internal waves, after correcting for internal tides’ effects. In this study, we use the Regional Oceanic Modeling System (ROMS) to investigate the magnitude and characteristics of internal tidal influences at each observation site. Furthermore, by comparing the model results with actual observational data, we evaluate differences in oceanic characteristics—such as location and topography—among observation sites with varying levels of internal tides’ influence. This approach allows us to further elucidate the relationship between GNSS-A observation accuracy and ocean field disturbances. This research will contribute to the advancement of seafloor geodesy and demonstrates the applied research and interdisciplinary contribution of ROMS.

presentations.presentation_title: High-resolution Wave Climate and Extremes Over the Sunda Shelf Based on a Triple-nested Wavewatch Iii––singv Modelling System
presentations.presenting_author: XINGKUN XU (Tropical Marine Science Institute, National University of Singapore, Singapore (TMSI))
presentations.abstract: This study integrates ongoing work at the Physical Oceanography Research Lab (TMSI, NUS & TCOMS) into a unified, high-resolution framework to characterize wave climate and extremes over the Sunda Shelf. We use a triple-nested WAVEWATCH III system forced by 8-km SINGV-RCM winds: an outer basin-scale domain for monsoon forcing and remote swell, an intermediate South China Sea/Sunda Shelf domain, and an inner unstructured mesh reaching O(100–200 m) resolution in key straits and nearshore waters, including Singapore. A multi-decadal hindcast (early 1980s–mid-2010s), driven by SINGV-RCM dynamically downscaled from ERA5, is validated against multi-mission altimetry and available in situ data. On this basis, we quantify monsoon seasonality, interannual variability linked to large-scale climate modes, and sharp cross-shelf/along-strait gradients in wave height, period, and direction that require high resolution to resolve. For hazards, we estimate design wave heights and return levels with GEV and peak-over-threshold methods and report associated uncertainty. For climate impacts, the same system is forced by CMIP6-driven SINGV-RCM simulations under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 across near-, mid-, and late-century windows to project changes in mean and extreme conditions. Wave power flux is also derived as a first-order indicator of marine energy potential. The framework provides decision-relevant guidance for coastal risk assessment and long-term planning in Southeast Asia. presentations.session_chairs: Changming DONG (Nanjing University of Information Science & Technology) , Sung Yong KIM (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology)
presentations.presentation_title: Long-term Statistical Analysis of North Pacific Mesoscale Eddies Based on High-resolution Satellite Altimetry Data
presentations.abstract: Mesoscale eddies of O (10–100) km are ubiquitous features of the North Pacific, especially along strong western boundary currents such as the Kuroshio, where they redistribute momentum, heat, salt, nutrients, and CO₂, enhance mixing, and modulate current pathways and coastal environments. Quantifying their long-term statistics is therefore fundamental to physical oceanography and coastal engineering.We present a basin-scale assessment based on automated detection and tracking applied to gridded sea surface height and surface geostrophic velocity derived from high-resolution satellite altimetry (0.125° × 0.125°) spanning from January 1993 to May 2025. Eddies are identified with a vector-geometry detection method and tracked by a feature-based algorithm to ensure temporal continuity. We analyze both cyclonic and anticyclonic eddies, apply lifetime-based filtering to isolate long-lived events, and compile statistics of spatial distribution, polarity, size, and lifetime over the entire North Pacific domain. The results show that most eddies are short-lived, typically lasting several weeks, whereas a smaller fraction persists for several months or longer. Long-lived eddies are systematically larger in horizontal scale and are preferentially concentrated in regions where strong currents prevail. Cyclonic and anticyclonic eddies occur in comparable numbers, yet their lifetime and size distributions differ in a consistent manner across subbasins.These findings indicate that frequent generation and rapid decay dominate eddy activity over much of the basin, while in strong-current regions, instability and eddy-mean flow interactions favor the persistence of long-lived eddies. The combined use of high-resolution altimetry with automated detection and tracking provides a robust framework for quantifying long-term mesoscale eddy statistics. The resulting dataset offers a foundation for future investigations of eddy-current interactions, process-oriented model validation, and assessments of impacts on basin-scale circulation and coastal environments.

presentations.session_chairs: Changming DONG (Nanjing University of Information Science & Technology) , Sung Yong KIM (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology)
presentations.presentation_title: Effects of Wind Forcing Resolution on Extreme Wind Representation and Wave Simulations Under Tropical and Extratropical Cyclones
presentations.abstract: Accurate wind forcing is essential for regional oceanic numerical modelling, particularly for the simulation of extreme wave events generated by tropical and extratropical cyclones. While high-resolution atmospheric reanalysis datasets are increasingly available, the influence of wind forcing resolution on the representation of extreme winds and the resulting simulation of extreme waves across different regional cyclone environments remains insufficiently quantified.This study examines the effects of wind forcing resolution on extreme wind representation and wave simulations using an event-based regional modelling framework in two contrasting cyclone environments: extratropical cyclone-dominated southeastern Australia and tropical cyclone-affected eastern Philippines. Numerical wave simulations are conducted using the Simulating Waves Nearshore (SWAN) wave model, forced with five wind datasets derived from two reanalyses: ERA5 (0.25°, 1°) and BARRA-R2 (0.11°, 0.25°, 1°). Simulations are performed for 50 extreme wave events in each region, identified using a Peaks-Over-Threshold approach applied to existing ERA5 wave data at selected coastal and offshore sampling points.Results show that coarse-resolution wind forcing systematically underrepresents extreme wind speeds and leads to underestimation of extreme wave heights, with the largest discrepancies occurring in coastal regions where wind gradients at the land/sea interface are strongest. Resolution effects are more spatially consistent under extratropical cyclones, whereas tropical cyclone events exhibit greater variability due to compact storm structures and rapid radial wind decay. Very intense tropical cyclones, such as Typhoon Haiyan (2013), show pronounced sensitivity to wind forcing resolution, with higher simulated wave extremes at finer resolutions. Differences in resolution sensitivity between the two regions further suggest the influence of coastal geometry, topography, and dominant cyclone characteristics.These findings highlight the importance of high-resolution wind forcing for improving the reliability of regional wave simulations under extreme extratropical and tropical cyclone conditions, particularly in coastal regions where impacts are most severe.

presentations.session_chairs: Changming DONG (Nanjing University of Information Science & Technology) , Sung Yong KIM (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology)
presentations.presentation_title: Depth Dependence of Coral Bleaching Risk Based on Thermal‑stress Assessment
presentations.abstract: Coral bleaching has increased in frequency, extent, and duration worldwide. Coral assemblages in the Mesophotic Zone (MPZ, typically ≥ 30 m depth) have been proposed as genetic refugia for shallow corals through thermal buffering and larval supply, yet evidence for their effectiveness is regionally variable. Here we quantified depth‑resolved links between thermal stress and bleaching by computing Degree Heating Weeks (DHW) from daily three‑dimensional temperature fields in the JCOPE2M reanalysis and comparing these estimates with independent bleaching observations.In shallow water, DHW and bleaching exhibited a clear positive association, consistent with the widespread use of DHW as a predictor of bleaching severity. In contrast, at subsurface depths, the association was weak or absent, indicating that a cumulative surface‑derived thermal metric alone is insufficient to predict bleaching below the surface. We also found that surface‑based DHW tends to underestimate the effective subsurface heat stress, underscoring that depth is not uniformly protective and that MPZ communities do not consistently function as refugia. These patterns are consistent with a greater role for processes such as thermocline displacement, internal‑wave cooling, and interactions with the light environment that modulate subsurface heat exposure and physiological stress. Our findings argue for an expanded framework beyond conventional surface‑based heat‑stress metrics, integrating depth‑resolved thermal diagnostics with site‑specific physical setting and genetic connectivity to improve conservation and adaptation planning for the MPZ and adjacent shallow reefs.

presentations.presentation_title: Three-Ocean Influences on Southeastern Pacific MHWs under Super El Niño Conditions
presentations.institution: Nanjing University of Information Science & Technology
presentations.abstract: Strong marine heatwaves (MHWs) in the southeastern Pacific are closely linked to super El Niño events, with a 70% occurrence probability under super El Niño conditions. Using fully coupled and partially decoupled CESM experiments, this study quantifies the remote modulation of strong southeastern Pacific MHWs by the tropical Indian Ocean and Atlantic under super El Niño conditions, and elucidates the key physical mechanisms through which the three-ocean regulate MHW intensity. During the developing winter of El Niño, Indian Ocean Dipole-like sea surface temperature anomalies enhance southeastward-propagating atmospheric wavetrains, together with intensified El Niño and its southward-extending teleconnection, thereby reinforcing anticyclonic anomalies over the southeastern Pacific. These circulation anomalies alter cloud cover and surface winds, increasing shortwave radiation and reducing sensible and latent heat loss, which favors MHW development. In contrast, the tropical Atlantic primarily affects the decay phase, as basin-wide warming weakens El Niño–related teleconnections and suppresses anticyclonic anomalies, leading to reduced MHW intensity. Overall, the tropical Indian Ocean enhances MHW intensity by 19.2%, whereas the tropical Atlantic reduces it by 21.7%. This study reveals the important role of cross-basin basin interactions in the evolution of MHWs in the southeastern Pacific.

presentations.session_title: Sea-level Variability and Impacts in the Asia-pacific
presentations.convener: Timothy SHAW (Centre for Climate Research Singapore) timothy_shaw@nea.gov.sg
presentations.session_chairs: Timothy SHAW (Centre for Climate Research Singapore) , Tanghua LI (City University of Hong Kong) , Jun'ichi OKUNO (National Institute of Polar Research)
presentations.presentation_title: Contrasting Influences of ENSO and IOD on Sea Level Variability Across the Singapore Strait and Peninsular Malaysia
presentations.abstract: This study investigates long-term sea level trends and interannual variability in the Singapore Strait, along the Peninsular Malaysia, and in the Malacca Strait during 1984–2020. The analysis integrates tide-gauge observations, satellite altimetry, and Delft3D model simulations forced by ERA5 atmospheric fields. Mean sea level trends across the region indicate a consistent rise of approximately 3.5–4.5 mm yr⁻¹, consistent with regional and global sea level rise estimates. Climate-driven variability is examined using detided sea level anomalies in relation to large-scale climate modes, focusing on the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO), the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD), and the Interdecadal Pacific Oscillation (IPO). The results reveal a clear east–west contrast in the dominant climate controls across the Singapore Strait. Sea level variability in the eastern Strait shows a strong association with ENSO, represented by the Southern Oscillation Index. Significant positive correlations (up to ~0.8) indicate elevated sea levels during La Niña conditions and reduced levels during El Niño events, reflecting ENSO-driven changes in regional winds, circulation, and monsoon strength. In contrast, sea level variability in the western Singapore Strait and the Malacca Strait is more strongly influenced by the IOD. Significant negative correlations (up to ~−0.6) suggest that positive IOD phases are associated with lower sea levels in the western Strait, highlighting the role of Indian Ocean forcing. The IPO modulates these relationships at decadal timescales by influencing the background frequency of ENSO phases. We have found that ENSO-driven Pacific forcing dominates in the eastern Singapore Strait through oceanic wave propagation and monsoon modulation, while IOD-driven waves control variability in the western Strait via the Malacca Strait pathway. Overall, the findings emphasize the importance of spatially varying climate drivers in shaping sea level variability in the dynamically complex Singapore Strait region.

presentations.convener: Timothy SHAW (Centre for Climate Research Singapore) timothy_shaw@nea.gov.sg
presentations.session_chairs: Timothy SHAW (Centre for Climate Research Singapore) , Tanghua LI (City University of Hong Kong) , Jun'ichi OKUNO (National Institute of Polar Research)
presentations.presentation_title: Partnership for Ocean Level Monitoring: Reinforcing Technical Capacity of Water Level Data Collection, Processing and Analysis for Climate Hazard Management in the Bangladeshi Delta.
presentations.abstract: Geographically, 2/3 of Bangladesh lies in a vast deltaic plain, formed at the mouth of the Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna rivers (GBMD), being the largest and most populated in the world, covering approximately 150,000 km² and home to more than 150 million inhabitants. Floods are frequent, and each year, during the summer monsoon, between 20% and 60% of the country is submerged. Today, more than 10% of the GBMD is less than one meter above mean sea level and land therein is subsiding, as in the largest deltas of the tropical areas. However, the data available to analyze these phenomena are still very limited in Bangladesh and virtually no data is transmitted to decision-making institutions in real time. This project, called “Partnership for Ocean Level Monitoring” (POLM), has the main objective of strengthening the technical capacities for observing variations in sea level rise and land level. It is based on the use of GNSS stations, to determine in a coupled manner the water (by Interferometric Reflectometry) and land levels. Our project aims to technically support the national institutes dedicated to the study of these parameters and involved in climatic hazards’ management, through: 1. deploying innovative and affordable sensors; 2. establishing a real-time data transfer network; and 3. contributing to the training of the local actors, especially female scientists. POLM will enable several proofs of concept adapted to the economic and technical realities of Bangladesh: a low-cost assembly of stations, which reduces costs by ~50%; and the use of 4G networks, well adapted to the country's satellite coverage, to ensure real-time data transmission. Preliminary results from the analysis of the collected water level measurements, their processing and quality assessment will be presented, as well as their experimental utilization in numerical models for the representation of the sea level dynamics.

presentations.presentation_title: Linking Paleo and Modern Sea-level Change In southeastern China
presentations.abstract: Sea-level rise, a pressing consequence of climate change, threatens substantial socio-economic risks to densely populated coastal regions across the world. Understanding the physical mechanisms driving the sea-level budget across different timescales is vital for coastal resilience. Yet, paleo sea-level budget studies have historically been largely disconnected from modern analyses due to disparities in time scales, variability, and data sources. In this talk, I will introduce recent works to bridge this divide in southeastern China through a comprehensive geological sea-level budget reconstruction with rigorous validation against diverse paleo-environmental records. This work situates contemporary sea-level trends within their broader geological context, revealing that paleo sea-level data and reconstructions are critical for understanding the modern sea-level hazards we face today.

presentations.convener: Timothy SHAW (Centre for Climate Research Singapore) timothy_shaw@nea.gov.sg
presentations.session_chairs: Timothy SHAW (Centre for Climate Research Singapore) , Tanghua LI (City University of Hong Kong) , Jun'ichi OKUNO (National Institute of Polar Research)
presentations.presentation_title: Sea Level Reconstructed from geological archives from Far Field Sites Since the Last Interglacial to Understand Ice Sheet Stability
presentations.abstract: The rapid melting of the polar ice sheets is a pressing issue for modern societies because many major cities around the world are located less than ten meters above sea level. Relative sea level change, or the change in sea surface elevation relative to land, is determined by a combination of global and local environmental and geophysical factors. Reconstructing past sea level histories is key to better understanding ice sheet stability in relation to climate change. Thus, improving the quality of sea level observation and modeling data is necessary. To estimate global ice volume changes, it is crucial to obtain evidence from biofacies that relies on in situ fossil material and grew at specific, shallow-water depths close to ocean shorelines during its lifespan. A time series is also necessary to estimate the exact timing of past sea levels by determining geological sequences, and dating must be done on the in situ fossil organisms themselves. Recent developments in sampling and analytical technologies have revealed detailed pictures of past sea levels when the global climate and mean sea level (GMSL) were lower than they are today, including during the last glacial maximum when GMSL was lower by 120 to 130 meters. In this presentation, I will share some of our new findings based on coral reefs located far from former ice sheets, where there are few glacio-isostatic adjustment (GIA) effects. This includes a potential solution to the missing ice problem, the magnitude of meltwater pulses, and the rate at which the GMSL dropped. Additionally, I will introduce a new method to reconstruct the behavior of past ice sheets using marine archives.

presentations.convener: Timothy SHAW (Centre for Climate Research Singapore) timothy_shaw@nea.gov.sg
presentations.session_chairs: Timothy SHAW (Centre for Climate Research Singapore) , Tanghua LI (City University of Hong Kong) , Jun'ichi OKUNO (National Institute of Polar Research)
presentations.presentation_title: Constraining Last Glacial Maximum Sea Levels Using a Global Database
presentations.abstract: Following the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) around 26-20 ka ago, sea levels rose by ~140-120 m. However, questions remain about the timing and magnitude of barystatic sea level rise. Discrepancies exceeding 25 m exist between ice volumes predicted by ice-sheet models and those inferred from relative sea level (RSL) records, which are corrected for glacial isostatic adjustment (GIA) to isolate the barystatic signal. This "missing ice" problem may stem from limitations in GIA models, including simplifications in Earth's structure and rheology, and from the quality and quantity of far-field LGM RSL constraints influenced by local processes not captured by GIA corrections.This study systematically reexamines far-field LGM records following the HOLSEA protocol, incorporating new data from the Argentine Shelf, Comoro Peninsula, the Atlantic coast of Africa, and the Chinese mainland coast from ~30 ka and ~15 ka. We correct RSL estimates using an ensemble of GIA predictions from commonly used ice-sheet models and account for local processes like tectonic uplift and subsidence.Our preliminary analysis focuses on the Bonaparte Gulf and Northwest Shelf (Australia) and Barbados (Caribbean) records. Applying a spatio-temporal statistical model on the Australian record indicates a lowstand of −103.7 ± 5.6 m at ~19.9 ka. For Barbados, Orbicella annularis (large living depth range of ±10 m) suggest lowstand timing between 26-19 ka, while Acropora palmata (narrower living depth range of ±2.5 m) constrain RSL to −102.6 ± 7 to −113.5 ± 4 m during 20-19 ka. After correcting for tectonic uplift and GIA, the Barbados and Australian records yield barystatic sea level estimates of 108-128 m, and 101-117 m respectively, consistent with ice-sheet volume estimates of 114 ± 9 m. These findings potentially can reconcile model-data discrepancies and provide improved constraints on the magnitude and timing of barystatic sea level at the LGM.

presentations.presentation_title: Holsea Datahub: an Open-source Web Portal for Global Relative Sea-level Data Since the Last Glacial Maximum
presentations.abstract: Here, we present the HOLSEA Datahub, an integrated web portal designed to facilitate the standardized synthesis of relative sea-level (RSL) reconstructions since the Last Glacial Maximum. This comprehensive database comprises over 15,000 validated index and limiting points spanning all continents, enabling broad spatial comparisons that minimize bias. The database structure clearly distinguishes between primary observations and their interpretations, allowing datasets to be refined as methods and theories advance.The portal provides dynamic visualization tools and statistical frameworks to explore spatiotemporal patterns of RSL change. Through an interactive interface, users can query and analyze datasets based on geographical location, chronology, and indicator type. This standardized approach enables robust comparisons between diverse sea-level indicators, from sedimentary sequences to biological and archaeological remains. A structured submission protocol, real-time data validation and peer-review process ensures consistent data quality and uncertainty assessment across contributions. The portal's collaborative infrastructure facilitates synthesis of datasets for large-scale analyses of ice-sheet sensitivity, solid Earth deformation, and sea-level projections. Integration with existing RSL databases enhances the temporal and spatial coverage of available records.The HOLSEA Datahub marks a significant advance in the standardization and accessibility of RSL data, providing essential constraints for understanding Earth system responses to deglaciation. This unified database will support robust statistical analyses of rates and mechanisms of RSL change, ultimately improving our ability to project future sea-level rise.

presentations.presentation_title: Southeast Asia Sea Level: Paleo Constraints, Modern Acceleration and Future Risk
presentations.abstract: Low‑lying equatorial coasts require an integrated evidence chain to prepare for rising relative sea level (RSL). Synthesizing Southeast Asian records, we build an end‑to‑end framework from paleo constraints to probabilistic projections. On the Sunda Shelf, post‑Last Glacial Maximum RSL rose ~121 m, with peaks ~15 mm yr⁻¹, reshaping ~2.3 million km² of paleo landscapes. Early‑Holocene rise (−21 m to −1 m, 10–7 ka) was followed by a +4 m mid‑Holocene highstand (~5 ka) and subsequent fall, exposing misfits with ice sheet models that imply other local to regional processes are at play. Indonesian coral microatolls and Singapore data archaeology halve modern RSL uncertainties, showing near‑stable RSL (0.08 ± 0.09 mm yr⁻¹) from the late 19th century to 1993, followed by an acceleration to 4.03 ± 0.13 mm yr⁻¹. Vertical land motion corrected projections for Singapore yield a likely (17th–83rd percentile) rise of 0.75 m (0.58–1.04 m) by 2100 (high‑emissions). A fused model‑based and expert‑informed workflow provides a single distribution with a 95th‑percentile of 2.2 m by 2100 under high emissions. Even under moderate emissions, projected rates are only surpassed during past abrupt ice‑loss events ~14.5 and ~9 ka. This linked framework connects past, present, and future coastal risk.

presentations.presentation_title: Response of the South China Sea Circulation to Sea Level Changes in the Northwestern Pacific
presentations.abstract: The slope current in the northwest South China Sea (SCS) plays a vital role in regulating mass and nutrient exchange between the coastal region and the open ocean. Over the past three decades, this current has exhibited a significant increasing trend, indicating a much stronger marginal sea-open ocean interaction. Using observational data, we show that the intensified anticyclonic warm eddy shedding from the Luzon Strait propagates along the continental slope, leading to a stronger slope current. During 1993-2022, a reduction in Subtropical Mode Water was accompanied by decreases in sea surface height (SSH) and Kuroshio transport in the Luzon Strait, as well as an enhanced looping pathway of the Kuroshio in the northern SCS. These conditions favor anticyclonic warm eddies (positive SSH anomaly) shedding from the northwestern Luzon Strait and propagating along the continental slope southwestward. At the same time, the companying cold eddies (negative SSH anomaly) propagates westward towards western SCS. The combined propagation of these dipole-like eddies further strengthens the SSH gradient between the shelf and inner ocean in the SCS, thereby intensifying the slope current. Importantly, it is the increased mean strength of the anticyclonic eddies, rather than their number, that drives this long-term current intensification. In contrast, neither local surface wind nor buoyancy forcing can account for the observed enhancement of the slope current, although wind forcing likely contributes to strengthening its southern segment. These findings highlight the crucial role of Kuroshio intrusion and eddy-current interaction in regulating the long-term variability of circulation in the SCS.

presentations.session_title: Oceanic Submesoscale Processes and Their Dynamical and Biogeochemical Impacts
presentations.convener: Zhiwei ZHANG (Ocean University of China) zzw330@ouc.edu.cn
presentations.presentation_title: Role of Submesoscale Stirring in Driving Lateral Dispersion and Vertical Exchange within a Cyclonic Mesoscale Eddy
presentations.abstract: Quantifying the role of submesoscale stirring in oceanic transport remains a central challenge in physical oceanography, owing to its small spatial scales and short temporal variability. Here, we investigate how submesoscale processes regulate lateral dispersion and vertical exchange within a cyclonic mesoscale eddy, using a combination of submesoscale-permitting in situ observations and high-resolution numerical model output. By analyzing the observed water-mass variability along cross-eddy isopycnals, this study reveals distinct dispersion regimes across depth, indicating strong depth-dependent transport pathways. In the eddy subsurface layer, we estimate an effective along-isopycnal submesoscale diffusivity exceeding 100 m² s⁻¹, highlighting the efficiency of submesoscale stirring in eroding lateral tracer gradients. To further elucidate transport mechanisms, Lagrangian particle tracking experiments are performed using LLC4320 model output, revealing pronounced lateral spreading and vertical penetration that vary with depth and position relative to the eddy core. In the mixed layer, submesoscale instabilities drive vigorous lateral dispersion, rapidly exporting tracers away from the eddy interior. In contrast, in the stratified subsurface layer, enhanced vertical shear associated with internal wave motions promotes isopycnal submesoscale stirring, leading to erosion of eddy coherence and enhanced vertical tracer exchange. Together, these results demonstrate that submesoscale stirring plays a fundamental role in driving both lateral and vertical transport in mesoscale eddies, with important implications for eddy trapping efficiency and water-mass evolution.

presentations.convener: Zhiwei ZHANG (Ocean University of China) zzw330@ouc.edu.cn
presentations.presentation_title: A Global Assessment of Eddy-wave Interactions in the Oceanic Forward Energy Cascade
presentations.abstract: The ocean is a complex fluid system containing dynamic motions across a wide range of spatial scales. The forward energy cascade governs the transfer of kinetic energy from larger to smaller scales, crucial for determining the pathway to ultimate ocean energy dissipation. While regional studies suggest eddy-wave interactions play an important role in driving the forward cascade, their contributions across regions and seasons remain unquantified, leaving a critical gap in our global understanding. Based on submesoscale-permitting global ocean simulations, we show that the dominant contributor to the most effective forward cascade is the self-type interactions, i.e., the eddy-eddy interactions in winter and wave-wave interactions in summer. However, this does not diminish the importance of cross-type, eddy-wave interactions. Noting that self-type interactions only cascade energy within their respective type of motions and do not influence the energy cascade of the complementary type, where cross-type eddy-wave interactions play the dominant role. Specifically, eddy-wave interactions in winter (summer) govern the cascade of wave (eddy) energy. Our findings identify the specific regimes where eddy-wave interactions are crucial for the forward cascade, offering insights into the relative contributions of self-type and cross-type interactions from a global statistical perspective.

presentations.convener: Zhiwei ZHANG (Ocean University of China) zzw330@ouc.edu.cn
presentations.presentation_title: Subsurface Anticyclonic Eddies in the Eastern South Pacific Ocean Imaged by Seismic Oceanography Method
presentations.abstract: Subsurface eddies are a key component of eastern boundary upwelling systems, yet their structure and dynamics remain poorly constrained by observations. Using multichannel seismic reflection data combined with simultaneous shipboard ADCP measurements, we investigate subsurface submesoscale anticyclonic eddies observed offshore of southern Chile in February 2017. Seismic imaging provides high‐resolution constraints on the vertical structure and horizontal scales of the eddies, particularly their lateral boundaries. Based on the eddy geometry resolved from seismic imaging and coincident velocity observations, we conduct quantitative analyses of the eddy velocity structure and momentum balance. The estimated Rossby numbers indicate strongly ageostrophic dynamics, and a comparison of centrifugal and Coriolis terms shows that the radial momentum balance of both eddies is governed by gradient wind balance rather than geostrophic balance. The joint observations further reveal a strong poleward Peru–Chile Undercurrent (PCUC) near 44°S, with velocities of 0.1–0.2 m s⁻¹, characterized by a distinctive seismic reflection signature along the continental slope. The spatial relationship among the eddies, the undercurrent, and local bathymetric curvature provides new observational evidence that subsurface anticyclonic eddies in eastern boundary upwelling systems can form through flow separation of the poleward undercurrent. Real oceanic eddies often exhibit complex, high-order structures that deviate significantly from simplified, axisymmetric models. Using a synergistic dataset of multi-channel seismic reflection data, vessel-mounted ADCP, satellite altimetry, and in-situ hydrological observations collected in early 2017, we analyze a subsurface anticyclonic eddy's three-dimensional fine structure in the eastern South Pacific Ocean and its spatiotemporal evolution. Our results reveal this eddy with a planar elliptical shape and a radially asymmetric tangential velocity distribution. Vertically, the eddy exhibits a distinct dual-core structure with an eastward-tilting axis and is surrounded by developing submesoscale spiral arms. High-resolution seismic transects further elucidate the non-uniformity of the internal water mass.

presentations.convener: Zhiwei ZHANG (Ocean University of China) zzw330@ouc.edu.cn
presentations.presentation_title: Multi-stage Development within Anisotropy Insight of an Anticyclone Eddy in Northwestern South China Sea in 2021
presentations.abstract: Mesoscale eddies help regulate ocean energy cascades. Eddies deformation influences barotropic instability, which represents kinetic energy transfer between scales; however, the barotropic instability structure has not been well studied. We investigated an intra-thermocline eddy (ITE) and developed a novel anisotropic method to examine the horizontal barotropic instability. The development of the ITE was monitored using a state-of-the-art autonomous underwater vehicle from May to July. The ITE became trapped in June and moved eastward in July. Based on anisotropic theory, the barotropic instability was separated into isotropic and anisotropic productions. The anisotropy contained information regarding shape and mean flow feedback of the eddy. Barotropic instability was the main source for ITE eastward propagation and was dominated by anisotropic production. Following a shape and anisotropy change, the ITE gained the mean-flow kinetic energy by the anisotropy shear production in June and by the anisotropy stretch production when moving eastward in July.

presentations.convener: Zhiwei ZHANG (Ocean University of China) zzw330@ouc.edu.cn
presentations.presentation_title: Spatiotemporal Variations of Mixed Layer Instability Intensity in the World Ocean Estimated Using Argo Float Observations
presentations.institution: Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Oceanic submesoscale circulations are driven by several mechanisms such as frontal shear instability, interactions with topography, and mixed layer instability. The mixed layer instability is a baroclinic instability occurring within the mixed layer, which generates rich submesoscale circulations in the winter in the mid-latitude. In the process of the instability, available potential energy in the upper ocean is released and transformed into kinetic energy at the submesoscale. Therefore, the energy release is closely linked to the instability intensity. In this study, the energy release in the world ocean is estimated from the mixed layer depth and horizontal buoyancy gradient based on a simple method proposed by Fox-Kemper et al. (2008) using monthly Argo float observation at a horizontal resolution of 1 degree from 2004 to 2024. The seasonality of the energy release exhibits the enhanced mixed layer instability around the major currents and in the subtropics in the mid-latitude of the winter hemisphere, which suggests a possibility to diagnose the spatiotemporal variations of submesoscale circulations. Furthermore, the regression analyses of the energy release against climate variation indexes exhibit the spatiotemporal variations of mixed layer instability intensity at interannual timescales. For example, El Niño events modulates the intensities in the subtropical Northeastern Pacific in the boreal winter, and around the Antarctic Circumpolar Current in the central Pacific and to the south of Australia in the austral winter. In addition, El Nino events can modulate the intensities in the tropical instability waves region in the tropical tropics. These results suggest possibilities that the available potential energy release estimated from various data at a coarse resolution such as CMIP data diagnose the spatiotemporal variations of mixed layer instability intensity in the world ocean at various timescales.

presentations.convener: Zhiwei ZHANG (Ocean University of China) zzw330@ouc.edu.cn
presentations.presentation_title: Current Feedback Is Promoting Subduction at Submesoscale Front While Killing Eddies
presentations.institution: Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Air-sea interactions are driven largely by momentum and heat exchanges at the sea surface. One of the mechanisms recently highlited is current feedback (CFB). CFB refers to the effect of wind stress considering the relative speeds of wind and sea surface currents, and it has been shown to significantly attenuate the kinetic energy of mesoscale eddies known as “Eddy Killing”. With CFB, even spatially uniform winds over the front can induce Ekman suction and pumping over the front. By considering geostrophic and ageostrophic shear stress at the surface balancing the wind stress, Ekman suction and pumping can arise even without wind. On the other hand, recent studies showed that the vertical component of relative vorticity near the surface frequently attains larger positive values at submesoscale compared to negative ones due to stretching of the relative vorticity on the dense side of the frontogenetic front. Despite these intrinsic characteristics of the submesoscale front, how CFB at submesoscale fronts affects vertical fluxes is not fully explored. In this study, submesoscale permitting simulations are conducted using to understand the effects of CFB in vertical exchanges in the Kuroshio Extension regions. We compared cases considering CFB and cases without it (NOCFB). The results show that cyclonic vorticity is much more enhanced at the surface front than anticyclonic vorticity, consistent with the previous studies. In addition, wind stress curl attains larger negative values with CFB on the dense side of the front than NOCFB case, leading to stronger downwelling. These results suggest that CFB has large implications not only for momentum and heat exchanges at the surface, but also for water mass subduction and biogeochemical cycles which have largely been overlooked thus far. As global warming may suppress the submesoscale activities, more accurate understandings and quantification of CFB induced subduction are necessary.

presentations.presentation_title: Seasonal Variability of Upwelling-favorable Winds and Mixed Layer Depth Controls Nutrient Bioavailability and Phytoplankton Growth at Submesoscale in Eastern Boundary Upwelling Systems
presentations.institution: Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Eastern Boundary Upwelling Systems (EBUSs) are the most biologically productive ecosystems worldwide, due to intense nutrient upwelling driven by equatorward winds. In most EBUSs, upwelling-favorable winds (UFW) peak during spring and summer, coinciding with maximum phytoplankton (Phy) biomass. However, the Northern Humboldt Region (NHR) exhibits a seasonal mismatch, with UFW peaking in austral winter while phytoplankton blooms typically develop in austral spring. This phenomenon is known as the Seasonal Paradox. In contrast, the Southern Humboldt Region (SHR) follows the canonical EBUS seasonal pattern, with aligned peaks in winds and phytoplankton growth. Despite these conditions, both regions sustain high net primary production.Previous studies have shown that under the seasonal paradox, Phy growth in the NHR is strongly constrained by vertical dilution associated with a deep winter mixed layer, and enhanced offshore advection, which together suppress blooming despite high nutrient availability. Nevertheless, the fate of nutrients within the mixed layer at submesoscales remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate how the seasonality of UFW modulates submesoscale processes that regulate nutrient bioavailability for phytoplankton uptake.To isolate the wind effects alone, and using the model CROCO coupled with a biogeochemical model BioEBUS, we conducted four simulations: (1) climatological conditions in SHR and (2) NHR, and (3) sSHR and (4) sNHR with wind seasonality shifted by six months for each, as an attempt to mimic the opposite region (sSHR mimicking NHR, sNHR mimicking SHR).Our results indicate that in the NHR case, the UFW prevents phytoplankton from reaching its maximum production potential, as evidenced by a lower yield compared to sNHR (NHR:sNHR ≈ 3:4). Conversely, in the SHR, maximum yield is achieved under climatological conditions, with reduced production in sSHR (SHR:sSHR ≈ 4:1). These contrasts are primarily driven by submesoscale dynamics enhanced by UFW, highlighting the strong sensitivity of EBUS productivity to wind seasonality.

presentations.session_title: Advancing Ocean Hazard Preparedness Through Science, Systems, and Society for Disaster Reduction Risk
presentations.convener: Suci Dewi ANUGRAH (The Agency for Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics) suci.anugrah@bmkg.go.id
presentations.session_chairs: Suci Dewi ANUGRAH (The Agency for Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics) , Megumi SUGIMOTO (The University of Osaka)
presentations.presentation_title: Advances in Tsunami Forecasting Method Using Various Observation Data
presentations.abstract: Tsunami forecasting methods have advanced greatly since the 2011 Tohoku-oki tsunami. The dense observation networks, including offshore ocean bottom pressure and seismic sensors (S-net, DONET, and N-net), have been installed in Japan. The dense Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) stations were also available worldwide. Now we use not only seismological data but also various data to forecast the tsunami height distribution accurately. The high-performance computational methods have also been advanced for real-time forecasting. Because of those advancements, “Digital Twin” is now recognized as a digital copy of the physical world stored in a digital space and used to simulate the sequences and consequences of a target phenomenon. In this paper, first, we developed a novel data assimilation method using dense ocean bottom pressure waveform data to improve the forecasted tsunami wavefield originally estimated from GNSS data using the REDARD method. Then that tsunami wavefield was used to compute the tsunami inundation along the coast using a high-performance computer for an accurate tsunami forecast as a Digital Twin. Results show that the data assimilation method significantly improves the tsunami wavefield; therefore, the forecasted tsunami inundation along the coast is also improved. We conclude that our novel data assimilation method is effective for real-time tsunami inundation forecasting. Second, a real-time tsunami hazard and damage forecast method for great earthquakes off the Pacific coast of Hokkaido in Japan was developed using the realistic scenarios that were constructed from various data, including slip distribution of historical great earthquakes, ocean-bottom crustal movement data, plate coupling rates, and a distribution of very low frequency earthquakes. Results show that the tsunami hazard and damages were significantly different for each scenario. Third, a tsunami forecasting method for volcanic tsunamis caused by the sector collapse was developed, particularly for the Krakatoa Volcano.

presentations.presentation_title: The Evaluation of Indonesian Tsunami Dissemination System, Response, and Multi-stakeholder Engagement Through Tsunami Simulation of the Iowave25
presentations.institution: The Agency for Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics
presentations.abstract: In 2025, the Agency of Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics (BMKG) conducted two tsunami simulation exercises to assess the performances of the dissemination system, response, and stakeholders participation in Indonesia specifically in the coastal Indian Ocean part. Three dissemination modes namely Warning Receiver System New Generation (WRS New Gen), Email, and SMS were employed to deliver early warnings to stakeholders. A set of evaluations were formed to observe the response of the Local Disaster Management Organization (LDMO) to tsunami warning and number of community engagement. The simulation's evaluation determined that the Warning Receiver System New Generation (WRS New Gen) is the most effective tsunami warning dissemination channel, with a delivery time of 1–3 minutes. Meanwhile, LDMO’s responses revealed four categories namely monitoring, coordinating, evacuation call, and dissemination. The simulations also successfully engaged a broad range of stakeholders, including Local and National government agencies, emergency services, community organizations, media, public places, private sector, and critical infrastructure. These results underscore the performance of the system and the need to strengthen the capacity of Local Disaster Management officers to respond appropriately and to maintain and enhance engagement.

presentations.abstract: We constructed 85 tsunami height poles in Aceh after the 2004 Sumatra tsunami, however 7 monuments are missing now. It means 77 monuments showing tsunami hazard risk as same as the 2004 Sumatra tsunami hight exists in Aceh. The monuments in Aceh are useful for memorial and awareness and records of tsunami-disaster prevent memory from wearing thin with time. However the decline in monuments has possibiliteis monuments may not have been effective in conveying the risk of tsunamis to future generations, as comuniteis were busy recovering from gigantic disaster. We have researched effects both Indonesia and Japan. It is easy for even outsiders and future people, to notice risk from the monuments as the same as tsunami high water at each location in the past disaster. In 2005 the project targets the following 8objectives :1. Encourage people to be prepared for the next disaster.2. Keep the memory of tsunami attack.3. Educate next generation with important lessons from the tsunami.4. Mourn the people who have passed away and to restore and reconstruct Aceh from the disaster.5. Keep accurate data of tsunami-height for future planning.6. Escaping sign with the tsunami height.7. Encourage people to live with hope and ease under tsunami risk. 8. Became a symbol of Aceh as the tsunami-attacked city.From 2025 we restarted to be awarding entries to the disaster education school competition in which students and teachers in Aceh use these tsunami memorials, in order to raise awareness of the tsunami memorials among comunities, provide sustenable disaster education, and maintain tsunami disaster awareness. Our rechallenges of presarving 77 tsunami monuments by community and disaster cultures in this resarch finally.

presentations.presentation_title: Tsunami Early Warning System Based On In-Situ Pressure Observation Network: Theory and Experiment
presentations.abstract: Significant variations in ground surface pressure associated with major tsunamis have been observed both near (e.g., Arai et al., 2011) and far from the source regions (e.g., Mikumo et al., 2008). These variations represent atmospheric Lamb waves trapped near the ground surface and propagating at the speed of sound, excited by vertical sea-surface displacement at tsunami onset. Numerical integrations of a compressible atmospheric model (e.g., Nakajima, 2019) have shown that not only the amplitude but also the waveform of atmospheric Lamb-wave pressure signals provides a robust indicator of tsunami characteristics, whose performance is largely insensitive to tsunami rise time. This property suggests that pressure observations may complement existing methods for tsunami hazard assessment, including events generated by slow fault motion.To realize this potential, three challenges must be addressed. Atmospheric Lamb waves can be generated not only by tsunamis but also by vertical ground motion associated with fault rupture. In addition, background pressure noise of meteorological origin must be removed, while barometric pressure variations may arise from vertical motionsat the sensor site itself.Here, we present approaches to address these challenges. First, fault motion preceding the initial tsunami wave is considered as a Lamb-wave source, rather than the tsunami sea-level change. Second, we investigate the use of a dense barometric network comprising several tens of sensors deployed within a compact region (~30 km), in which pressure time series are dynamically exploited to semi-empirically predict regional pressure variations of meteorological origin. Also, integrated analysis of the dense barometric network allows pressure components associated with local vertical ground motion to be extracted and removed. Such a dense barometric network consisting of low-cost MEMS sensors has been operated in Fukuoka City for about one year, and its feasibility for tsunami-related hazard applications is evaluated using observed pressure observations.

presentations.presentation_title: Effect of Virtual Reality Based Tsunami Evacuation Training on Route Selection Behavior
presentations.abstract: During the 2009 American Samoa Earthquake and Tsunami, residents who had participated in evacuation drills possessed knowledge of vertical evacuation and were able to recall evacuation sites, and interviews confirmed the effectiveness of such drills. Since the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake, disaster education and evacuation drills focusing on residents’ evacuation behavior have been increasingly emphasized. Furthermore, the adoption of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030 at the Third United Nations World Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction in 2015 positioned the promotion of proactive evacuation behavior and the enhancement of community-based disaster risk reduction as key pillars, leading to increased global discussion on tsunami evacuation. Although evacuation drills have been shown to have the potential to reduce evacuation delays and casualties, participation rates remain low due to physical and time constraints. In this study, we examined whether evacuation drills using virtual reality (VR) could complement conventional evacuation drills. The results indicate that participants without prior familiarity with the area were more likely to reach the nearest evacuation site after experiencing VR-based evacuation training. Analysis of correct route-selection rates at each decision point revealed that the lowest accuracy occurred at the starting point, followed by Y-shaped intersections. At the target Y-shaped intersection, the designated evacuation route had a narrower road width than the alternative route, which was wider; thus, participants may have intuitively chosen the wider road, resulting in a lower correct selection rate. In contrast, other Y-shaped intersections exhibited higher accuracy, as the branching roads had similar widths, reducing the influence of road width on decision-making and facilitating selection of the designated evacuation route. Future work should involve a larger number of participants and analyses that account for route complexity.

presentations.session_title: Oceanic Mesoscale Dynamical Processes and Climate Effects
presentations.convener: Tongya LIU (Second Institute of Oceanography, Ministry of Natural Resources) liutongya@sio.org.cn
presentations.session_chairs: Linlin ZHANG (Institute of Oceanology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) , Kun ZHANG (Tongji University)
presentations.presentation_title: Global ocean and sea ice variability simulated in eddy-permitting coupled models: SINTEX-F3 and CMIP6 HighResMIP
presentations.institution: Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Ocean mesoscale eddies with a horizontal scale of approximately 100 km play a prominent role in global ocean heat transport which regulates the Earth’s climate. However, most climate models cannot fully resolve the ocean mesoscale eddies due to computational resource constraints. To mitigate this limitation, a new eddy-permitting climate model with an ocean resolution in the order of 25 km, SINTEX-F3, was developed. Compared to other eddy-permitting climate models in the CMIP6 HighResMIP, SINTEX-F3 demonstrates a cold bias in the mid-high latitudes and a weaker El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO). Despite these model biases, SINTEX-F3 reproduces other tropical climate phenomena such as the Atlantic Niño/Niña well, indicating that these modes are less dependent on ENSO in the model. In the subtropical-midlatitudes, SINTEX-F3 also captures the mesoscale sea surface temperature and surface heat flux variability well, particularly in the western and eastern boundary current regions. Furthermore, SINTEX-F3 simulates the mean state and variability of sea ice in the Antarctic Sea more accurately than the Arctic Sea, probably because of the improved sea-ice model physics as well as the increased model resolutions. While further efforts are needed to address the cold bias and the weaker ENSO representation in SINTEX-F3, resolving ocean mesoscale eddies may help improve simulating and predicting global ocean and sea ice variability in climate models.

presentations.convener: Tongya LIU (Second Institute of Oceanography, Ministry of Natural Resources) liutongya@sio.org.cn
presentations.session_chairs: Linlin ZHANG (Institute of Oceanology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) , Kun ZHANG (Tongji University)
presentations.presentation_title: Enhanced Eddy Activity in the Retreating Arctic Marginal Ice Zone: Observations and Implications
presentations.institution: Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology
presentations.abstract: Oceanic eddies play a crucial role in polar climate dynamics, influencing heat transport, biogeochemical cycles, and sea ice distribution. The present study is focused on investigating mesoscale and submesoscale eddy activity in the Marginal Ice Zone of the Russian Arctic Seas and Fram Strait, examining their dynamics, three-dimensional structure of eddies, and their influence on the ice formation and melting processes. Moreover, we present a new methodology for automatic eddy detection in the MIZ regions. The automated detection of eddies in the (MIZ) remains a significant challenge due to the complex interplay of oceanic and atmospheric processes and the limitations of traditional observation techniques. This study presents an advanced machine learning framework for the automatic detection and classification of mesoscale and submesoscale eddies in the Arctic MIZ using high-resolution Sentinel-1 synthetic aperture radar (SAR) data. We employ YOLO-based deep learning models to detect and differentiate cyclonic and anticyclonic eddies under diverse environmental conditions. The models are trained on region-specific datasets and optimized through extensive augmentation techniques to enhance performance in ice-covered waters.Analysis reveals reduced sea ice concentration over anticyclonic compared to cyclonic eddies, attributable to enhanced melting/freezing rates, partially offset by ice convergence/divergence processes.Additionally, we investigate three‐dimensional structures of mesoscale and submesoscale eddies in MIZ of Fram Strait by collocating the eddy detection results from SAR with temperature and salinity data from the multiple platforms (research vessels, autonomous profiling floats). This work advances automated remote sensing methodologies and provides valuable insights for understanding eddy dynamics in polar oceans, aiding future climate modeling efforts. This research was supported by the Russian Science Foundation (project 25-47-01005).

presentations.convener: Tongya LIU (Second Institute of Oceanography, Ministry of Natural Resources) liutongya@sio.org.cn
presentations.session_chairs: Linlin ZHANG (Institute of Oceanology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) , Kun ZHANG (Tongji University)
presentations.presentation_title: Modulation of Upper-Ocean Shortwave Heating by Mixed Layer Depth and Chlorophyll associated with Tropical Instability Waves
presentations.abstract: Tropical Instability Waves (TIWs) are mesoscale (~1000 km) features that modulate upper-ocean temperature in the equatorial Pacific by reorganizing mixed layer depth (MLD) and chlorophyll, thereby altering the absorption of shortwave radiation. However, the respective contributions of chlorophyll and MLD pathways in regulating mixed-layer temperature remain poorly quantified. This is partly because fully interactive ocean–ecosystem models involve two-way coupling, in which biologically induced changes in mixing and circulation further modify the biological fields, obscuring the individual contributions of chlorophyll and MLD. Here, an offline ocean-ecosystem model is used to isolate chlorophyll-induced radiative effects from associated dynamical adjustments, rather than relying on a fully interactive model, enabling a clearer attribution of chlorophyll versus MLD contributions. In addition, a novel reconstruction and compositing approach for TIWs is introduced to extract coherent TIW signals and robustly link them to shortwave-heating anomalies. Focusing on the TIW-active region, three contributions to TIW-associated mixed-layer temperature anomalies driven by shortwave heating are quantified: (1) the direct chlorophyll effect, whereby chlorophyll modulates the attenuation of shortwave radiation and hence its absorption within the mixed layer; (2) the direct MLD (heat-capacity) effect, whereby MLD sets the effective heat capacity, such that a deeper mixed layer yields a weaker temperature tendency for the same net heat input; and (3) an indirect MLD effect, whereby TIW-induced MLD changes modify the chlorophyll content within the mixed layer and thus further modulate mixed-layer shortwave absorption. This pathway-based decomposition provides a quantitative framework for interpreting TIW-related thermodynamic variability associated with shortwave heating. It is shown that heat capacity effect related to MLD variations (pathway (2)) emerges as the dominant contribution and predominantly increases mixed-layer temperature, whereas pathway (3) tends to act with the opposite sign. Pathway (1) also warms the mixed layer but plays a secondary role.

presentations.session_title: Oceanic Mesoscale Dynamical Processes and Climate Effects
presentations.convener: Tongya LIU (Second Institute of Oceanography, Ministry of Natural Resources) liutongya@sio.org.cn
presentations.session_chairs: Linlin ZHANG (Institute of Oceanology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) , Kun ZHANG (Tongji University)
presentations.presentation_title: Dominant Inverse Nonlinear Energy Cascades in Coastal and Inner Shelf Waters
presentations.abstract: Ocean turbulence has been identified as a key driver in the transportation of mass, including heat and nutrients. These processes are of paramount importance for the regulation of the planet's climate and the preservation of marine ecosystems. The South China Sea is a region characterised by strong tidal forcing and monsoonal variability, and the understanding of how energy cascades across scales remains an open challenge. While mesoscale eddies are known to contain the majority of oceanic kinetic energy, the mechanisms that link their generation, transfer, and dissipation are not yet fully understood. Our analysis employs high-resolution numerical simulations to investigate cross-scale energy and enstrophy transfers on the inner shelf of the South China Sea, with a focus on the interplay between tidal and wind-driven forcing. A coarse-grained analysis was employed to assess the direction and intensity of turbulent energy cascades. The results obtained demonstrate a dominant inverse energy cascade, indicating energy transfer from smaller to larger scales. Seasonal variability further contributes to the shaping of these dynamics. During summer, stronger southwest winds and river discharge enhance nonlinear energy exchanges and mixing efficiency. On the other hand, in winter conditions, quasi-steady, tidally dominated flows prevail. The present study provides a comprehensive analysis of the mechanisms by which wind and tidal forcings control energy pathways across scales, thereby establishing a link between small-scale turbulence and large-scale circulation. These findings contribute to the advancement of knowledge regarding the potential influence of climate-driven changes in monsoon or tidal strength on ocean mixing, which may have consequences for the accuracy of regional climate prediction and the management of coastal ecosystems.

presentations.convener: Tongya LIU (Second Institute of Oceanography, Ministry of Natural Resources) liutongya@sio.org.cn
presentations.session_chairs: Linlin ZHANG (Institute of Oceanology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) , Kun ZHANG (Tongji University)
presentations.presentation_title: Formation of a Quasi-universal Internal Wave Spectrum by Wind Forcing Alone: Idealized Modeling and Mooring Observations
presentations.institution: South China Sea Institute of Oceanology
presentations.abstract: Oceanic internal waves (IWs) play a key role in diapycnal mixing that sustains the global overturning circulation. Their energy follows a quasi-universal Garrett-Munk (GM) spectrum, traditionally attributed to nonlinear wave-wave interactions under combined wind and tidal forcing. However, growing evidence points to the importance of eddy-wave interactions, but the specific energy contributions from mesoscale and submesoscale motions to this GM spectrum remain unclear. More importantly, the generation of this GM spectrum by eddy-wave interactions has not been observed in the real ocean. In the present work, an idealized numerical model is used to simulate the formation of a GM-like spectrum by eddy-wave interaction under wind forcing alone. Energy transfers are diagnosed in both Eulerian and Lagrangian coordinates using a multi-scale energy and vorticity analysis. It is found that IW energy supplied by mesoscale eddies is comparable to that from submesoscale motions in Lagrangian coordinate, whereas this mesoscale contribution appears much weaker in Eulerian coordinate. Vertically, mesoscale eddies transfer energy to IWs in the upper ocean, while this energy transfer is reversed in the pycnocline. The forward transfer is driven by wave capture, whereas the reverse transfer arises from critical-layer effects. In-situ mooring observations from the Southern Ocean further support the role of eddies in facilitating the generation of a GM-like spectrum under wind forcing alone. Together, these findings clarify the energy pathways through which mesoscale and submesoscale dynamics energize IWs and offer new insight into the dynamical processes that help maintain the GM spectrum.
