presentations.convener: Tongya LIU (Second Institute of Oceanography, Ministry of Natural Resources) liutongya@sio.org.cn
presentations.session_chairs: Linlin ZHANG (Institute of Oceanology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) , Kun ZHANG (Tongji University)
presentations.presentation_title: Ocean-scale interactions in the Northwest Pacific in a submesoscale-permitting model
presentations.abstract: Ocean circulations strongly interact with each other and transfer energy across horizontal scales. These ocean-scale interactions control the ocean energy budget and hence the variability of large-scale circulations and climate. The Northwest Pacific has rich multi-scale circulations due to interactions between the Kuroshio, eddies, and bottom topography. Focusing on this region, we assess the spatiotemporal variation of oceanic kinetic energy (KE) cascade, and more importantly, clarify the dependence of forward energy cascade on the bottom topography as well as the underlying mechanisms, using a submesoscale-permitting ocean general circulation model (OGCM). The surface KE spectrum and cross-scale KE flux are computed based on a novel coarse-graining approach. The results show that in the open ocean with a flat bottom, downscale KE flux concentrates in strong fronts driven by convergent flows, indicating that frontogenesis is the dominant mechanism of forward energy cascade. Both submesoscale KE and forward energy cascade peak in winter, when strong mixed-layer instability releases available potential energy from mesoscale fronts, and subsequent interactions among mixed-layer eddies drive secondary frontogenesis. In regions where the complex bottom topography, including small islands and seamounts, and the Kuroshio coexist, forward energy cascade at submesoscales is attributed to intense flow-topography interactions, which leads to barotropic instability on the lee side of topography as indicated by the sign change of barotropic potential vorticity gradient. Seasonal cycle of submesoscale KE and KE flux in these regions depends on the strength of flow-topography interactions related to the Kuroshio conditions. Furthermore, the model results are compared with those derived from gridded altimetry products and a mesoscale-resolving OGCM, raising cautions on interpreting the energy cascade computed with different dataset. This study reveals the distinct roles of frontogenesis and flow-topography interactions in the energy cascade in the Northwest Pacific, providing insights into the energy pathway in the ocean.

presentations.convener: Tongya LIU (Second Institute of Oceanography, Ministry of Natural Resources) liutongya@sio.org.cn
presentations.session_chairs: Linlin ZHANG (Institute of Oceanology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) , Kun ZHANG (Tongji University)
presentations.presentation_title: High-resolution Observations Reveal Structural and Dynamic Differences Between Surface and Subsurface Anticyclonic Eddies in the Southeast Pacific
presentations.abstract: Mesoscale eddies are fundamental carriers of oceanic kinetic energy and crucial agents for the transport of heat, salt, and biogeochemical tracers. While satellite altimetry effectively monitors surface-intensified features, the detection and characterization of subsurface-intensified eddies, and their distinction from surface modes, remains a significant observational challenge. This study presents a systematic comparison of the vertical structure and dynamics of a Surface Anticyclonic Eddy (SAE) and two Subsurface Anticyclonic Eddies (SSAEs) observed in the Southeast Pacific in 2017.By utilizing high-resolution Multi-Channel Seismic (MCS) reflection sections (~10 m horizontal resolution) combined with vessel-mounted ADCP (vmADCP), satellite remote sensing, and underway hydrographic observations, we resolved the fine-scale structure of these distinct eddy types. The SAE exhibited a pronounced positive Sea Surface Height (SSH) anomaly, accompanied by positive SST, SSS, and pCO₂ anomalies, and a negative Chl-a anomaly. On the seismic sections, the SAE appeared as a bowl-shaped reflection structure extending downward from the surface, collocated with a near-surface velocity maximum.In contrast, the SSAEs showed weak or negligible surface signatures; specifically, a smaller and deeper submesoscale coherent vortex (SCV) identified in the seismic data was undetectable by standard satellite products. The seismic imaging revealed a distinct convex lens geometry for the SSAEs which corresponded precisely to subsurface velocity maxima. Furthermore, while acoustic backscatter indicated that zooplankton distribution was primarily driven by diel vertical migration, secondary modulations were observed. These were likely driven by strong vertical motions at eddy edges and distinct water mass properties within the subsurface eddy core. These findings demonstrate the efficacy of joint seismic and hydrographic observations in resolving the "blind spots" of satellite oceanography, offering new perspectives on the coupling mechanisms between the dynamics and biogeochemistry of oceanic eddies.

presentations.session_title: Indo-pacific Ocean Circulation and Interocean Exchange: Dynamics and Climate Impacts
presentations.convener: Shijian HU (Hohai University) sjhu@qdio.ac.cn
presentations.session_chairs: Tomoki TOZUKA (The University of Tokyo)
presentations.presentation_title: Imminent Rapid Decline of the Indonesian Throughflow After Reaching a Turning Point of Co2 Concentration
presentations.abstract: The Indonesian Throughflow (ITF) represents the only tropical inter-ocean pathway of global ocean circulation and plays a central role in the Earth’s climate system. Climatemodels suggest that the ITF would beweakened under global warming, but historical observations indicate a contradictory trend. Here using CMIP6 simulations, we find that the response of the ITF to increasing atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) concentration is nonlinear and exhibits an abrupt rapid decline after surpassing a turning point. The ITF’s decline can be explained by the response of its halosteric and thermosteric components to rising CO2 levels associated with changes in winds and precipitation. The current level of CO2 concentration has reached the turning point, indicating that a rapid decline of ITF and a transition of the Indo-Pacific state is likely imminent despite the remaining uncertainties. These findings have implications for understanding climate tipping elements and global ocean circulation under global warming.

presentations.session_chairs: Tomoki TOZUKA (The University of Tokyo)
presentations.presentation_title: A Linear Inverse Modeling Framework for Investigating ENSO-IOD Interactions and Its Application to CMIP6 Models
presentations.abstract: Tropical basin interactions strongly influence the evolution of tropical sea surface temperature (SST), with air–sea coupling playing a central role. Here we assess how interbasin coupling and air–sea interactions shape interannual climate variability in the tropical Indian Ocean (IO) and Pacific Ocean (PO) using a linear inverse model (LIM) framework constructed from SST and 10-m zonal wind (u10) anomalies in the two basins. In stochastically forced, cyclostationary LIM simulations with systematically varied interbasin coupling strength, the amplitude of El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) increases as IO–PO interactions weaken, consistent with a delayed negative feedback from the IO onto ENSO. In contrast, Indian Ocean dipole (IOD) variability decreases as interbasin coupling is reduced; however, the IOD persists even in the fully decoupled limit, supporting the view that it is an intrinsic mode of IO variability. Applying the same framework to CMIP6, we diagnose inter-model diversity by classifying models according to LIM stability under different coupling configurations. Models in the stable group exhibit smaller ENSO biases, whereas models that become unstable when the IO and PO are fully decoupled tend to show larger ENSO variability biases. Finally, we identify a 3–6-month lead of ENSO forcing bias onto the IOD as a potential pathway contribute to overly persistent ENSO and associated IOD biases in CMIP6. Overall, this LIM-based approach provides a compact, process-oriented tool for probing Indo–Pacific coupling mechanisms and evaluating coupled model fidelity.

presentations.session_chairs: Tomoki TOZUKA (The University of Tokyo)
presentations.presentation_title: The Role of Wind in Driving the Subsurface Velocity Maximum of Makassar Strait Throughflow and Mindanao Current
presentations.abstract: For most wind-driven ocean currents, velocity is typically surface intensified with a peak at the surface. However, in a notable exception, the Makassar Strait throughflow (MST) and the Mindanao Current (MC) - two dynamically linked boundary currents - exhibit their maximum velocities in the subsurface (upper thermocline) layer. In this study, the driving mechanisms of subsurface velocity maxima are investigated, using mooring observations, ocean reanalysis products, and regional model simulations, with particular emphasis on the role of wind forcing. Both the in situ measurements and reanalysis data show that the subsurface velocity maxima in the MST and MC in boreal summer are stronger and shallower than in winter. We find that the higher-order baroclinic modes (Modes 3 and 4) are crucial in shaping vertical structure of velocity and forming the subsurface velocity maximum. The meridional dynamic height difference along MC is identified as a driver of the subsurface velocity maximum, through balancing with frictional forces. The zonal density gradient, being negative at the surface but positive at depth, is consistent with the subsurface velocity maximum. Numerical experiments with a regional model indicate that the sea surface winds play an important role in driving the seasonality of subsurface velocity maxima of the MC and MST. Wind stress causes downwelling (upwelling) over the MC and deepens (lifts) zero-contour of horizontal density gradient, and leads to a deeper (shallower) subsurface velocity maximum. Wind forcing can also influence the subsurface velocity maximum of MST by modulating the seasonal freshwater transport from the South China Sea.

presentations.presentation_title: Ocean Stratification in the Indonesian Throughflow During Marine Isotope Stage 11
presentations.institution: Faculty of Earth Sciences and Technology, Institut Teknologi Bandung
presentations.abstract: The Indonesian Throughflow (ITF) serves as a pathway for water masses that play an important role in transferring heat and low-salinity water from the Pacific Ocean to the Indian Ocean in low-latitude regions. This study aims to analyze and compare the seasonal conditions of ocean stratification in Indonesian waters, particularly along the western and eastern ITF routes, during the Marine Isotope Stage (MIS) 11 and Pre-Industrial (PI) periods based on the results of a comprehensive coupled climate model. The results show good agreement between the model outputs and proxy data for the MIS 11 period, as well as with the COBE-SST2 satellite dataset for the PI period. Seasonal analyses were conducted using temperature and salinity parameters processed vertically to a depth of 300 m, along with calculations of vertical gradients and density data to evaluate water column stability using the Brunt–Väisälä frequency (N²). The results indicate that during MIS 11, strong stratification occurred, as thermocline layers formed in all four transects (2 transects each in the western and eastern ITF routes) at depths ranging from 50 to 75 m with higher temperature gradients of about 0.05–0.125 °C/m. N² values > 0 in all transects indicate a stable and strongly stratified water column, based on both spatial and seasonal variations. Water column stability was generally higher during MIS 11 compared to PI along the western ITF route during the southeast monsoon (anomaly value of 1.20 × 10⁻⁴ N2) due to the influence of heat accumulation and monsoonal winds. In contrast, during the northwest monsoon, water column stability in MIS 11 was lower along the eastern ITF route (anomaly value of –7.72 × 10⁻⁵ N2) due to higher global temperatures and local factors such as rainfall, ITF intensity, and upwelling, as well as atmospheric conditions.

presentations.session_chairs: Yu-Lin TSAI (National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University) , Yun-Ta WU (National Cheng Kung University) , Peter Hong-Yueh LO (National Taiwan University (03734301)) , Huabin SHI (University of Macau)
presentations.presentation_title: Solitary Wave Interaction with a Vertical Cylinder Over a Viscous Mud Bed: CFD, Laboratory Experiments, and Shallow-water Modeling
presentations.abstract: Seabeds with muddy sediments are found around the world. While sand consists of coarser particles and demonstrates noncohesive behavior, mud consists of finer particles and demonstrates cohesive behavior. Therefore, the physical processes involving waves and sand must be modeled differently from those involving waves and mud. A muddy seabed is known to attenuate water waves, yet how it impacts wave-structure interaction remains understudied. This study considers the solitary wave interaction with a vertical cylinder situated on a viscous mud bed, which is modeled as a thin layer of Newtonian fluid on the seabed. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations show that although the viscous mud bed attenuates the incident wave as expected, the inclusion of the mud bed increases the net horizontal force exerted on the vertical cylinder, due to wave-induced mud flows. Using a clear silicone fluid to approximate the viscous mud layer, laboratory experiments were performed. Water surface profiles, mud surface profiles, velocity fields, and horizontal forces exerted on the vertical cylinder were measured and used to validate the numerical simulations. Lastly, a one-way (water-to-mud) coupled linear shallow water wave model was constructed and shown to be capable of predicting the mud-wave-cylinder interaction satisfactorily and efficiently. The shallow-water model can be used as a preliminary tool for efficiently predicting the wave force increase due to the viscous mud layer.

presentations.presentation_title: Decadal Evolution of the Qigu Sandbar and Its Impacts on Storm-surge Inundation in Southwest Taiwan
presentations.institution: Department of Hydraulic and Ocean Engineering, National Cheng Kung University
presentations.abstract: Barrier sandbars provide essential natural protection for lagoon-backed coasts in southwest Taiwan by attenuating waves and storm surge. The Qigu sandbar system offshore Tainan has experienced pronounced multi-decadal change driven by alongshore sediment transport, inlet migration, and extreme typhoon events, resulting in a progressive weakening of its natural barrier function. Since 2011, extensive restoration efforts have been implemented in the Qigu system. More than 40 projects carried out between 2011 and 2024 dredged approximately 1.26 million m³ of lagoon sediment and restored about 96 hectares of sandbar area. Satellite-based analyses indicate that, at the most erosive sector of the sandbar, the mean shoreline retreat rate decreased from approximately 50 m/yr during 1994–2009 to less than 6 m/yr after restoration, demonstrating that targeted nourishment and sandbar rehabilitation can substantially slow long-term erosion. To quantify how continued morphological evolution affects coastal hazard, we coupled long-term morphodynamic projection using the Coastal Modeling System (CMS) with storm-surge inundation simulations using the Sedimentation and River Hydraulics (SRH) model. CMS cross-section diagnostics indicate a clear north-eroding, south-stable pattern: the northern sector shows a landward migration of the 0 m contour of approximately 350 m over a 10-year period, whereas the southern sector exhibits less than 70 m of change over the same timeframe. For the Qigu domain, SRH simulations under a 100-year design sea state, where wave height is 15.62 m and wave period is 15.81 second, indicate that sandbar narrowing and offshore deepening shift the breaker zone landward and intensify storm-surge inundation hazard, expanding inundation extent and increasing flood depths for lagoon-adjacent, low-lying settlements. A coastal protection strategy involving targeted elevation of the sea dike at the identified hotspot effectively eliminates the local inundation concentration, highlighting the benefits of focused reinforcement at high-risk locations.

presentations.presentation_title: Estimating Drag and Inertia Coefficients in Solitary Wave–vegetation Interaction: from Laboratory Experiments to Nonhydrostatic Modeling
presentations.abstract: Coastal wetlands (e.g., mangroves) are increasingly regarded as effective natural buffers that attenuate wave energy and reduce coastal hazards, supporting the growing adoption of nature-based solutions for coastal protection. Even though vegetation can effectively attenuate waves, predictive modeling remains challenged by substantial uncertainty in quantifying vegetation-induced hydrodynamic resistance. To assess how different force-based parameterizations represent wave–vegetation physics, we compare flume measurements against non-hydrostatic numerical simulations within a consistent framework. In the flume, solitary waves were generated and allowed to propagate through an idealized patch of submerged, rigid stems. Free surface elevations were recorded using wave gauges, and hydrodynamic forces were measured using instrumented single-stem load cells placed at randomly selected locations within the patch and an integrated patch-scale total force measurement, respectively. Depth-averaged velocities associated with solitary waves were reconstructed from measured free surface time series using solitary-wave theory. The drag (CD) and inertia (CM) coefficients were then inversely estimated via least-squares fitting of the Morison equation. The inferred coefficients were incorporated into the vegetation module of the non-hydrostatic wave-flow model, SWASH, to simulate solitary-wave propagation through the vegetation patch. Simulations benchmarked against measurements show that coefficients inferred from either force-measurement approach can reproduce the observed free surface evolution upstream and downstream of the patch for the tested condition. Their differences motivate further analysis of scale effects and within-patch spatial variability in vegetation loading. Ongoing work extends the analysis to a broader range of solitary wave conditions (e.g., wave height and water depth) to clarify how the coefficients should be estimated and to provide practical guidance on parameter selection for predictive simulations of wave–vegetation dynamics.

presentations.presentation_title: Scaling Analysis of Radially Spreading Gravity Currents Under Sustained Injection
presentations.abstract: This study presents a theoretical framework for understanding radial gravity current propagation sustained by constant volumetric discharge. Employing conservation principles and front-condition constraints, we derive self-similar solutions that characterize the spatial and temporal evolution of the flow. Our findings reveal that depth attenuation follows h~X-2/3 along the radial coordinate, accompanied by front deceleration scaling as Uf~X-1/3 Temporal integration yields X∼t3/4 for front advancement. These analytical results establish a coherent theoretical foundation for predicting spreading behavior in continuously fed axisymmetric flows.

presentations.presentation_title: Spatial Visualization and Assessment of Wave Energy in Taiwan: the Northeastern Coast and Taichung as Case Studies
presentations.abstract: Taiwan, an island with a maritime climate, experiences wave environments strongly modulated by the southwesterly monsoon and typhoons in summer and the northeasterly monsoon in winter, leading to pronounced regional and seasonal variability. As wave energy is a promising renewable resource closely linked to climatic forcing, a systematic assessment integrating numerical modeling and observations is essential.This study combines the WAVEWATCH III (WW3) model provided by the National Academy of Marine Research with in situ wave buoy observations to analyze wave conditions at monthly, seasonal, and interannual scales. The intensity and spatiotemporal variability of wave energy under different seasonal regimes, including the winter northeasterly monsoon and the summer southwesterly monsoon and typhoon periods, are quantitatively evaluated, with case studies focused on the northeastern coast of Taiwan and the Taichung region. Results indicate that the winter northeasterly monsoon produces the most stable and highest wave energy potential along the northeastern coast, highlighting its suitability for wave energy development. These findings enhance understanding of the linkage between seasonal atmospheric forcing and wave energy variability, and provide scientific support for renewable energy planning and coastal energy resource assessment in Taiwan.

presentations.session_chairs: Yu-Lin TSAI (National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University) , Yun-Ta WU (National Cheng Kung University) , Peter Hong-Yueh LO (National Taiwan University (03734301)) , Huabin SHI (University of Macau)
presentations.presentation_title: High-fidelity Numerical Investigation of Surge–tide Interaction Along Western Taiwan Using Data-driven Asymmetric Typhoon Wind Forcing
presentations.abstract: Accurate storm surge prediction critically depends on the realism of atmospheric wind forcing, particularly in coastal regions characterized by complex topography. In the Northwestern Pacific, typhoon circulations interacting with steep terrain frequently exhibit persistent asymmetric deformation, commonly referred to as terrain-modulated or topographic locking effects. These asymmetries are poorly represented by conventional symmetric parametric wind models, limiting their applicability for high-fidelity coastal surge simulations.In this study, we develop a physically constrained parametric typhoon wind-field framework that explicitly accounts for terrain-induced asymmetry through data-informed pattern synthesis. A regional wind-field archive is constructed using ECMWF ERA5 reanalysis, including sea level pressure and 10-m wind fields for 282 typhoon events affecting Taiwan during 1980–2023. For a given storm configuration, the framework quantifies the relative contribution of historical analogs via a designed weighting scheme and synthesizes a two-dimensional asymmetric wind field through weighted blending, while preserving physical consistency without the need for high-resolution dynamical atmospheric downscaling.The proposed framework is evaluated using typhoon cases traversing the mountainous terrain of Taiwan. Nearshore wind structures generated by the model are systematically compared with ERA5, and the resulting wind fields are further coupled with the COMCOT-SS storm surge model to assess surge response. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach reproduces reanalysis-consistent asymmetric wind patterns near complex coastlines and yields storm surge simulations comparable to those driven directly by ERA5 forcing. Additional experiments using wind-field archives derived from numerical weather prediction hindcasts further indicate the transferability of the framework across different data sources.Overall, this study presents a computationally efficient and physically grounded wind-field modeling approach that bridges data-driven pattern extraction and high-fidelity numerical storm surge simulation. The framework provides a practical pathway toward improved predictive capability for coastal flooding in regions where terrain-modulated cyclone structure plays a dominant role.

presentations.convener: Yun-Ta WU (National Cheng Kung University) ytwu@gs.ncku.edu.tw
presentations.session_chairs: Yu-Lin TSAI (National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University) , Yun-Ta WU (National Cheng Kung University) , Peter Hong-Yueh LO (National Taiwan University (03734301)) , Huabin SHI (University of Macau)
presentations.presentation_title: Effects of Gap Geometry and Installation Angle on Permeability Characteristics of Flap-gate
presentations.abstract: Previous studies have demonstrated that a flap-gate breakwater is effective in mitigating tsunami and storm surge impacts and exhibits sufficient structural stability. When the gate is in the upright position, watertightness is ensured by rubber seals that fill the gaps between gates. However, quantitative evaluation of the flow passing through the gaps while the gate is operating in an inclined position has not been sufficiently quantified. In this study, hydraulic model experiments were conducted under the critical condition in which the watertight rubber seals were removed. The effects of gap geometry and installation angle on the flow rate through the gap were investigated. The experiments were performed under steady-flow conditions with varying initial water depths to reproduce different water-level conditions between the offshore and harbor sides. Two gap geometries were considered: a “cylindrical–rectangular column” configuration that represents the actual flap-gate structure, and a “rectangular–rectangular column” configuration in which geometric asymmetry was eliminated. For each geometry, installation angles of 45°, 60°, and 90° were tested, and the flow rate through the gap was estimated from measured water-level differences. For the flap-gate-type geometry, an increasing trend in the flow rate through the gap was observed as the installation angle decreased from 90°. Similarly, for the rectangular–rectangular geometry, although no significant difference was found between 45° and 60°, the flow rates through the gap under these inclined conditions were higher than those at 90°. These results suggest that, although further investigation of energy loss due to flow contraction is required, it is feasible to estimate permeability as a function of water-level difference and installation angle. Future work will focus on developing a permeability model based on experimental results and implementing the permeability effect of flap gates into tsunami propagation models for harbor regions.

presentations.presentation_title: Experimental And Numerical Analysis Of The Stability Of Gabions As Armoring Units For Composite Breakwater Mounds
presentations.abstract: Recently, gabions have attracted significant attention as armor units for composite breakwater mounds due to their secondary functions as seaweed beds and artificial reefs. While previous experimental studies have demonstrated their effectiveness, few have investigated the direct relationship between hydrodynamic forces and the stability of gabion units. This study aims to clarify the failure mechanisms of gabions by evaluating the flow and pressure fields in detail using numerical analysis and to validate the results of hydraulic model experiments.The hydraulic model experiments were conducted at a scale of 1/40, considering both regular and irregular waves based on Froude’s similitude law. For the numerical analysis, the 3D numerical wave tank CADMAS-SURF/3D was employed, where each part of the structure was modeled using porosity, inertia coefficients, and drag coefficients. The numerical simulations replicated the regular waves used in the experiments to investigate the hydrodynamic forces acting on individual gabions based on the flow velocity and pressure distributions, which are difficult to measure experimentally.The main findings of this study are as follows: (1) In the hydraulic experiments, the gabions were observed to undergo uplift at the ocean-side shoulder of the crest when no gaps were provided between the armor units. Conversely, under conditions where gaps were present between units, sliding failure originating from the slope shoulder occurred prior to the uplift. (2) The numerical analysis generally reproduced the wave profiles and flow velocities observed in the experiments. Assessment of the overturning moment based on the calculated horizontal and vertical wave forces confirmed the validity of the uplift failure observed at the ocean-side crest shoulder. (3) Applying the flow velocities obtained from the numerical analysis to the Isbash formula revealed that the locations identified as having insufficient weight were consistent with the initial sliding points in the experiments.

presentations.convener: Yushi MORIOKA (Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology) morioka@jamstec.go.jp
presentations.session_chairs: Yushi MORIOKA (Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology) , Atsushi FUJIMURA (University of Guam) , Hsiao-Chun TSENG (National Taiwan Ocean University)
presentations.presentation_title: Realigning Marine Protected Area Governance with Earth System Principles
presentations.abstract: Marine biodiversity and coastal ecosystems continue to decline despite the proliferation of area-based management tools (ABMTs), particularly marine protected areas (MPAs). This failure stems from a governance landscape characterized by sectoral, polycentric, and fragmented institutional structures. When regulatory frameworks ignore the persistent uncertainties generated by dynamic human-environment interactions, they weaken sustainable development efforts and fail to mitigate the cumulative impacts of long-term anthropogenic stressors. This presentation addresses these challenges through the lens of Earth System Governance and the Anthropocene. While traditional MPA research often overlooks the causal links between Earth systems and governance outcomes, an Anthropocene legal perspective argues that regulatory systems must align with Earth science principles such as ecological integrity to remain functional. In an era of high anthropogenic intervention, ecological integrity must be redefined beyond traditional "no-take" zones to incorporate the co-evolutionary state of human-impacted natural systems as a primary indicator of ecosystem health. Furthermore, this perspective reveals critical disparities in the application of international environmental law. The principle of international cooperation, while foundational, varies in strength across different regimes, highlighting the persistent tension between "conservation" and "sustainable use." To prevent missing critical intervention windows under escalating climate pressures, this report re-evaluates the MPA governance framework. By identifying structural misalignments with Earth system principles, this study seeks to transform ineffective "paper parks" into resilient, equitable systems. Ultimately, successful governance requires a shift toward institutional learning, ensuring that legal norms reflect the interconnected realities of the Earth systems.

presentations.convener: Yushi MORIOKA (Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology) morioka@jamstec.go.jp

presentations.presentation_title: Seasonal Variability of Benthic Metabolism and Dissolved Organic Carbon Dynamics in a Tropical Seagrass Meadow
presentations.institution: National Kaohsiung University of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Seagrass meadows are highly productive coastal ecosystems that strongly regulate carbon cycling through benthic metabolic processes at the sediment–water interface. However, the sources and composition of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) in seagrass systems remain poorly understood. In particular, the coupling between benthic metabolism and DOC characteristics has rarely been examined, limiting our ability to constrain DOC production and transformation in coastal carbon budgets. In this study, we conducted seasonal measurements using core incubation in a tropical seagrass meadow to investigate benthic metabolism, DOC fluxes, and associated changes in DOC composition. Benthic metabolic rates, including gross primary production (GPP), respiration (R), net benthic community production (NCP), and the photosynthesis-to-respiration (P/R) ratio, together with DOC fluxes, were quantified. Our results reveal pronounced seasonal variability in benthic metabolism and DOC dynamics across both seagrass habitats and bare sediments. The P/R ratios were consistently greater than 1 throughout the year, indicating that seagrass habitats were net autotrophic and functioned as a net carbon sink. The highest NCP was observed in summer (146 ± 34.1 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹), whereas the lowest NCP occurred in spring (2.3 ± 15.1 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹). In contrast, the P/R ratios were consistently less than 1 in bare sediments, indicating net heterotrophic conditions and acting as a net carbon source. Seagrass habitats exhibited relatively higher benthic DOC fluxes compared to bare sediments. Significant correlations were observed between benthic metabolic rates and DOC fluxes across seasons, indicating a strong coupling between metabolic activity and DOC dynamics. In addition, protein-like DOM dominated the DOC composition in seagrass habitats, whereas humic-like components were predominant in bare sediments. These results highlight that seasonal shifts in benthic metabolic balance directly influence both the quantity and quality of DOC released from coastal sediments.

presentations.session_chairs: Yushi MORIOKA (Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology) , Atsushi FUJIMURA (University of Guam) , Hsiao-Chun TSENG (National Taiwan Ocean University)
presentations.presentation_title: Digital Twins of the Ocean for Sustainable Marginal Seas
presentations.institution: Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: The marginal seas of South and East Asia support highly productive ecosystems and coastal economies, yet they are increasingly vulnerable to extreme events arising from seasonal to interannual climate variability. Digital Twins of the Ocean (DTOs) provide an integrated framework to link marine science with sustainability by coupling observations, models, and user-oriented tools. This talk highlights DTO architectures developed within Japanese operational platforms, including Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology initiatives and the Japan Coastal Ocean Predictability Experiment, and their alignment with the OceanPrediction DCC. The talk reviews several operational and research modeling efforts across the marginal seas of South and East Asia and demonstrates how DTOs can be developed around these systems to better serve stakeholder needs. Emphasis is placed on multi-scale modeling frameworks that efficiently link basin-scale climate variability, monsoon forcing, and air–sea interaction with high-resolution coastal dynamics, enabling the representation and prediction of extremes such as marine heatwaves, anomalous circulation, and coastal flooding. When coupled with data assimilation, diagnostic analyses, and uncertainty-aware workflows, these systems retain predictable signals across timescales and translate them into actionable indicators, including marine heatwave intensity and duration affecting fisheries productivity, hazardous ocean conditions relevant to port and maritime operations, and early-warning information for coastal flooding and compound-event risk. Web-based interfaces and interoperable analysis tools support the delivery of these indicators in forms suited to fisheries management, maritime safety, and disaster risk reduction across Asian marginal seas.

presentations.session_title: Interdisciplinary Science on Coastal and Marginal Seas
presentations.convener: Yushi MORIOKA (Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology) morioka@jamstec.go.jp
presentations.session_chairs: Yushi MORIOKA (Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology) , Atsushi FUJIMURA (University of Guam) , Hsiao-Chun TSENG (National Taiwan Ocean University)
presentations.presentation_title: Kara Sea Freshened Surface Layer in 6 Global Ocean Reanalyses
presentations.abstract: The Kara Sea receives substantial freshwater discharge from the Ob and Yenisey rivers, producing a freshened surface layer. We evaluate how accurate six global ocean reanalyses—FIOCOM, HYCOM, GLORYS12, GLORYS2v4, C-GLORSv7, and ORAS5—represent this freshened layer. Sea surface temperature (SST) and sea surface salinity (SSS) are compared with satellite products for ice-free season in the Kara Sea (June–October) over 2019–2023. For each reanalysis, we compute monthly basin-wide SST and SSS fields biases with respect to satellite data and derive mean error (ME), mean absolute error (MAE), and root-mean-square error (RMSE), along with seasonal means for each year. SST errors are small across products (seasonal MAE < 0.5 °C; RMSE < 1 °C), likely reflecting SST assimilation implemented in the reanalyses. In contrast, SSS errors are substantially larger. FIOCOM shows the lowest seasonal errors (MAE 2.2–3.0 psu; RMSE 2.9–4.1 psu), whereas GLORYS2v4 exhibits the highest (MAE 3.4–5.7 psu; RMSE 4.6–6.9 psu); other products fall in between. Seasonal SSS difference maps indicate that all reanalyses underrepresent the Ob and Yenisey plumes, with local biases of 10–20 psu, implying inadequate reproduction of plume extent where satellites detect strong freshening. Potential causes include (1) sea-ice model errors and (2) misrepresentation of river runoff. For the Ob and Yenisey plumes, sea-ice meltwater contribution to total freshwater content is relatively low (~8% annually), therefore inaccuracies in runoff forcing can be the main cause of surface salinity errors. Global ocean reanalyses under consideration prescribe climatological runoff as a surface flux. This climatological data may be outdated and it neglects interannual variability. Moreover, runoff as a surface flux parametrization may misrepresent near-coastal plume dynamics. We suggest using gauge-based, time-varying discharge and representing river runoff as lateral boundary conditions to reduce SSS errors in the Kara Sea. This research was supported by the Russian Science Foundation (project 25-47-01005).

presentations.presentation_title: Bottom Cold Water Intrusion Events in the Bungo Channel Based on Field Observations in Summer 2021
presentations.abstract: The Bungo Channel, located between Shikoku and Kyushu in southwestern Japan, is a key strait connecting the Seto Inland Sea and the Pacific Ocean. Interactions between the Kuroshio Current and the continental slope near the Ashizuri Peninsula induce episodic intrusions of cold, nutrient-rich bottom water from the Pacific Ocean into the channel. These bottom cold water intrusion (BCI) events play an important role in sustaining coastal ecosystems and marine resources. This study examines the characteristics and driving mechanisms of BCI events using field observations conducted during the summer of 2021. Observations were conducted from May to August using three seabed-deployed Acoustic Doppler Current Profilers and Temperature–Salinity meters to monitor currents and near-bottom hydrographic conditions. CTD surveys were also used to capture the vertical structure of the water column. CTD observations revealed periodic BCI events propagating along the seabed at the outer station of the Bungo Channel, characterized by cold and slightly low-salinity water masses. TS meter data showed that BCI events occurred intermittently every 1–2 weeks, with individual events lasting 2–4 days and producing bottom temperature decreases of 0.6–0.9 °C per day. EOF and PC analyses identified a dominant current pattern during BCI events (Mode 1, explaining 59% of the variance), characterized by vertically stratified and countercurrent flows. BCI events were associated with northeastward currents at the outer and central stations, turning northwestward at the inner station. Equation of Motion analysis indicated that barotropic and baroclinic pressure gradient forces were the primary drivers of the intrusions. Notably, BCI events in summer 2021 occurred more frequently during spring tides, contrasting with previous studies reporting a preference for neap tides. These results provide new insights into the physical processes governing BCI in the Bungo Channel and contribute to an understanding of coastal ocean dynamics in the region.

presentations.session_title: Advances In Oceanic Data Assimilation Methodologies, Forecasting And Reanalysis
presentations.convener: Yuhang ZHU (Chinese Academy of Sciences) yhzhu@scsio.ac.cn
presentations.session_chairs: Yuhang ZHU (Chinese Academy of Sciences)
presentations.presentation_title: Machine Learning-based Covariance Correction for Ensemble Kalman Filter with Small Ensemble Size
presentations.abstract: Data assimilation (DA) integrates numerical model forecasts with observations to achieve optimal state estimation. Ensemble-based methods, such as the ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF), are widely used for state estimation in high-dimensional and nonlinear dynamic systems. However, their performance strongly depends on ensemble size, therefore causing a tradeoff problem between accuracy and computational cost. To address this problem, this study presents a machine learning-based EnKF framework that maintains high accuracy with a relatively small ensemble size. Specifically, a fully connected neural network (FCNN) is built to predict the difference between the forecast error covariances estimated from a small ensemble and a sufficiently large ensemble, with the latter being assumed to be an accurate representation of the truth. This predicted covariance correction is then incorporated into the EnKF via an elementwise scaling strategy, yielding a corrected forecast covariance that better approximates the true uncertainty level and sequentially produces more accurate analysis results. To demonstrate the feasibility and performance of the proposed algorithm, we perform a set of uumerical experiments with the Lorenz-63 and Lorenz-96 systems, and the results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm significantly outperforms the standard EnKF with the same small ensemble size, by achieving notably higher analysis accuracy while remaining computationally efficient. This approach provides a practical pathway to accurate and computationally efficient data assimilation for high-dimensional and nonlinear dynamic systems.

presentations.presentation_title: An Intercomparison of Eddy-resolving Ocean Reanalyses in the Western North Pacific
presentations.abstract: We performed an intercomparison of three eddy-resolving ocean reanalyses (FORA-WNP30, GLORYS12V1, and BRAN2020) for the western North Pacific over the period 1993-2016. While all three products exhibit high consistency in large-scale surface mean fields due to data assimilation, notable discrepancies are found in mesoscale variability and subsurface structures, reflecting differences in model configuration and assimilation schemes. FORA-WNP30, employing a four-dimensional variational (4D-VAR) scheme, exhibits high spatiotemporal variability in sea surface height (SSH). However, its sea surface salinity (SSS) variability is strongly dampened by a short restoring timescale. GLORYS12V1 retains intense coastal SSS variability due to the absence of strong surface restoring. However, it exhibits lower eddy kinetic energy levels compared to the others, likely due to dissipative viscosity parameterization. BRAN2020 shows systematic differences east of Japan, including reduced SSH variability and lower temporal correlations. These are attributed to its simplified bathymetry (capped at 5000 m), which eliminates topographic steering effects and alters eddy propagation speeds. Based on these findings, we will discuss how horizontal resolution is not the sole determinant of performance; bathymetry, subgrid-scale parameterizations, and boundary conditions play equally critical roles in reproducing regional ocean dynamics.

presentations.presentation_title: Deep Learning for Efficient Data Assimilation and Forecast Correction
presentations.abstract: Traditional ensemble-based data assimilation methods suffer from high computational costs and limited ability to correct model errors in long-term forecasts. This study introduces a unified deep learning framework combining “replacement” and “correction” strategies to jointly optimize initial conditions and reduce model error accumulation. Using the Lorenz-63 model, we develop DAMLP—a neural network that replaces the EnKF analysis step—and a neural error correct scheme that adjusts forecasts periodically without observations. Results show DAMLP lowers computational cost and improves initial conditions, while the correct scheme enhances long-term forecast skill. This work offers a scalable approach for efficient assimilation and forecasting in high-dimensional nonlinear systems.

presentations.presentation_title: Marine Microbes as the Biological Nexus Between Ocean and Atmosphere
presentations.abstract: Marine microbes are important players in the Carbon biogeochemical cycle in the ocean. Microbes act at the microscale, intimately “touching” molecules thus dictating the fate of the C and other elements. Now we know, that on a daily basis at the planetary level, Ocean and Atmosphere share water, gases and Microbes! Within my talk, we will explore the Ocean-Atmosphere connectivity mediated by marine Bacteria and Archaea along a complexity gradient from 1 liter to 12000 litres flume and from field work to a 2.2 cubic meter atmospheric chamber simulator. Finally, I will propose how Ocean-Atmosphere interaction knowledge is an asset to tackle the triple planetary crisis.

presentations.presentation_title: The Biogenic Sulfur Cycle in the Coupled Ocean-Sea ice-Atmosphere System
presentations.abstract: Polar oceans and sea ice regions are global hotspots for the production of biogenic volatile methylated sulfur (VMS) compounds: dimethyl sulfide (DMS) and methanethiol (MeSH). VMS compounds make important contributions to atmospheric particle formation and cloud property modulation, especially when polar atmospheres are pristine. As a result, the polar biogenic sulfur cycle may induce significant climate feedbacks in response to ongoing sea ice decline. However, polar VMS production, emission and atmospheric oxidation processes remain poorly represented in current numerical models, hampering assessments of their radiative impacts and, in turn, implementation of targeted observations necessary for predictive understanding of changes in the ocean–sea ice–atmosphere (OIA) system.The SCOR working group CIce2Clouds has been taking a proactive approach to untangle the existing gaps and provide a roadmap toward predictive understanding by synthesizing current knowledge of the polar biogenic sulfur cycle and its representation in models. We identify key features of sea ice habitats for biological VMS production, sea ice physical features that enhance or suppress VMS emissions, and atmospheric VMS oxidation at low temperatures that controls the contribution of oxidation products to particle formation or growth. These features are tightly coupled, emphasizing the need for coordinated efforts across disciplines that span the OIA interface, and among observational, experimental, and modeling communities. In the presentation, we will provide a concise overview of our synthesis paper [1]. presentations.presentation_title: Origins and Formation Process of Atmospheric Organic Aerosol in the Southern Sea of Okhotsk During the Phytoplankton Bloom in Spring
presentations.institution: Graduate School of Environmental Science, Hokkaido University
presentations.abstract: Marine organic aerosol (OA) affects regional climate through aerosol-radiation interactions including cloud formation. The Sea of Okhotsk is one of the most productive oceanic regions in the world, which is expected to be huge source of marine OA, particularly during the phytoplankton bloom in spring after the sea-ice retreat. To elucidate the origin and formation process of marine OA in this oceanic region, continuous sampling of submicrometer aerosols has been conducted at a coastal site in Mombetsu since August 2023. Chlorophyll a (Chl a) concentrations in surface seawater derived from in situ and satellite-based observations suggested more intense spring bloom in 2024 than in 2025. Aerosol mass concentration showed a peak during the bloom in 2024, which was higher than that in 2025. Organic matter (OM) (46±17%) and sulfate (31±9%) were dominant components of aerosols throughout the study period. Mass concentration of OM during the spring bloom in 2024 was significantly higher than that in 2025, which corresponded to the intense bloom in 2024. OM was highly water soluble, where water-soluble OM accounted for 68±11% and 85±8% of OM during the spring bloom periods in 2024 and 2025, respectively. During the bloom, aerosol water-soluble organic carbon (WSOC) was mainly attributed to highly-oxidized marine secondary OAs, which was suggested to be produced from α-pinene and dimethyl sulfide. The contribution of these marine biogenic secondary OAs to WSOC was more evident in 2024, which was linked to the intensity of bloom. This study suggests that the majority of OAs in the Sea of Okhotsk during the spring bloom is attributable to secondary OA associated with marine biota which is likely linked to the sea ice retreat. In particular, the intensity of bloom was suggested to control the mass of aerosol OM, which may influence the regional and potentially global climate.

presentations.presentation_title: Fast-growing Phytoplankton Influence Atmospheric Ice Nucleation and Cloud Properties
presentations.abstract: Sea spray aerosols contain ice-nucleating particles (INPs), which affect the formation and properties of clouds. In the laboratory, we show that aerosols emitted from fast-growing marine phytoplankton produce effective immersion INPs, which nucleate at temperatures significantly warmer than the atmospheric homogeneous freezing (−38.0 degrees C) of pure water. Both cyanobacteria and diatom monocultures, aerosol sampled over phytoplankton cultures induced ice nucleation at temperatures as high as −15.0 degrees C during exponential phytoplankton growth. In comparison, during the stationary and death phases. ice nucleation did not occur until colder temperatures (−28.5 degrees C and below). The ice nucleation at warmer temperatures was associated with relatively high values of the maximum quantum yield of photosystem II, an indicator of the physiological status of phytoplankton associated with the presence of cells with efficient photochemistry and greater potential for photosynthesis. For comparison, field measurements in the North Atlantic Ocean showed that high net growth rates of natural phytoplankton assemblages were associated with marine aerosol that acted as effective immersion INPs at relatively warm temperatures. Data were collected over 4 days at a sampling station maintained in the same water mass as the water column stabilized after deep mixing by a storm. Phytoplankton biomass and net phytoplankton growth rate (0.56 per) were greatest over the 24 hours preceding the warmest mean ice nucleation temperature (−25.5 degrees C). Collectively, our laboratory and field observations indicate that phytoplankton physiological status is a useful predictor of effective INPs and more reliable than biomass or taxonomic affiliation. Ongoing chemostat studies of continuous cultures with fixed growth rates are underway to further define the growth rate-ice nucleation connection. Ocean regions associated with fast phytoplankton growth, such as the North Atlantic during the annual spring bloom, may be significant sources of atmospheric INPs.

presentations.convener: Koji HAMASAKI (Atmosphere and Ocean Research Institute, The University of Tokyo) hamasaki@aori.u-tokyo.ac.jp
presentations.session_chairs: Koji HAMASAKI (Atmosphere and Ocean Research Institute, The University of Tokyo) , Yoko IWAMOTO (Hiroshima University) , Yuzo MIYAZAKI (Hokkaido University)
presentations.presentation_title: Seasonal Changes in Iron Sources to the Surface Ocean in the Subarctic Western North Pacific Revealed by Iron Isotopes
presentations.abstract: The Subarctic Western North Pacific is a high-nutrient, low-chlorophyll region, where primary production is limited by iron (Fe). Atmospheric deposition, including mineral dust and anthropogenic combustion, is a major source of Fe in the surface ocean, and Fe supply by dissolution of coastal sediments is also considered to be important. However, it remains unclear when these different Fe sources dominate and how their contributions change seasonally. In this study, we used stable Fe isotope ratios (δ56Fe) as tracers to distinguish Fe sources in aerosols and seawater and to investigate seasonal changes, from winter to summer, in Fe supply to the surface ocean. Aerosol and seawater samples were collected at station K2 (47ºN, 160ºE) during R/V Hakuho-maru cruises in early summer 2023 and R/V Mirai cruise in winter 2021. The δ56Fe of coarse aerosol particles was close to that of mineral dust regardless of season. In contrast, fine particles showed much lower δ56Fe, around –1‰ in winter and as low as –2.2‰ in summer. These low δ56Fe values indicate a significant contribution from anthropogenic combustion sources, with a larger relative contribution in summer than in winter. In surface seawater, dissolved Fe (DFe) concentrations were higher in winter and lower in summer, while δ56Fe showed the opposite seasonal trend. In winter, δ56Fe values in the mixed layer (except at the very surface) were similar to those in intermediate waters, suggesting a large contribution of Fe supplied upward from the intermediate depth, rich in sedimentary-derived Fe. At the surface, higher δ56Fe indicates an additional input of atmospheric Fe. In summer, changes in both concentration and δ56Fe can be explained by a combination of biological uptake and atmospheric Fe input.

presentations.session_title: Marine Environmental Changes in the Western Pacific and Its Marginal Seas: Roles of Global Climate Change Versus Anthropogenetic Impacts
presentations.convener: Jing ZHANG (University of Toyama) jzhang@sci.u-toyama.ac.jp
presentations.session_chairs: Chin-Chang HUNG (National Sun Yat-sen University)
presentations.presentation_title: Warming Impedes Zooplankton Recovery from an Effluent-driven Ph Decrease in a Tropical Coastal Ecosystem for Three Decades
presentations.institution: Graduate Institute of Marine Affairs, National Sun Yat-sen University
presentations.abstract: Coastal ecosystems are increasingly exposed to multiple stressors, particularly in the densely populated Asia-Pacific tropics. Zooplankton, owing to their small size and short life cycles, are especially vulnerable to environmental perturbations. In western Taiwan, coastal waters experienced a short-term effluent-driven decline in pH and sustained long-term warming. A three-decade zooplankton monitoring dataset provides a rare opportunity to disentangle community responses to effluent-driven pH decrease and evaluate the role of warming in shaping recovery trajectories. Changes in pH and temperature exerted nonlinear, taxon-specific effects on zooplankton abundance. Effluent-driven pH decrease led to marked declines across most groups, with recovery evident following the return of pH to baseline levels. However, warming modulated recovery dynamics that increasing temperatures accelerated recovery in some taxa (e.g., sea spackles and echinoderm larvae) while impeding others (e.g., copepods and shrimp larvae), resulting in altered community composition. These findings highlight the critical role of warming in mediating recovery under compound stressors, and underscore the importance of recovery or resilience, not merely sensitivity, in structuring zooplankton communities. Despite limitations, our results offer a foundation for refining predictive models and guiding future research on recovery mechanisms and interspecific interactions in planktonic systems under projected climate change.

presentations.session_chairs: Chin-Chang HUNG (National Sun Yat-sen University)
presentations.presentation_title: Dynamics of Water Masses and Nutrients in a Day on a Continental Shelf, Quantified Using Rare Earth Elements
presentations.abstract: East China Sea (ECS) provides essential biological resources for its local fishery and contributes to biodiversity on its surrounding seas, mainly through the Kuroshio Current (KC/KW), which regulates cross-shelf (CS) material transport on various scales. A range of phenomena is involved, and a different mix of processes occurs at each time and location, which makes CS exchanges complex and variable. Among the potential forces of CS exchanges in a continental shelf is the tide. We presented high-resolution time-series observations of heavy Rare Earth Elements (HREEs) combined with physical observations to elucidate tidal-induced temporal variabilities in nutrient transport at the shelf break of the ECS over a single tidal cycle. The results are: (1) Hydrodynamic processes influence the distribution of chemical and physical properties in the bottom water of ECS on an hourly basis. (2) Reintroduction of deep Kuroshio Water (KIW) during the onshore flow was notable for its high nutrient content. (3) During the observation, net DIN and DIP fluxes from the Kuroshio region (KW) were 5.59 and 6.69 times larger than the DIN and DIP fluxes from the continental shelf water (MSW) on a daily basis.

presentations.presentation_title: Integrated Real-time Habitat Forecasting and Fleet Behavior Modeling for Purse Seine Fisheries in the Western and Central Pacific Ocean
presentations.institution: Marine Science Oriented Ocean Technology Implementation Center, National Sun Yat-sen University
presentations.abstract: Skipjack tuna is the dominant commercial species in the Western and Central Pacific Ocean. Climate variability such as El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) poses significant challenges for fishing grounds identification and sustainable management. This study integrated fishery logbook data and global automatic identification system (AIS) effort data with satellite-derived environmental parameters to develop species distribution models. Our results indicate that the finer spatial resolution is optimal for empirical analysis, and logbook-derived fish yield data provide more reliable environmental associations and higher accuracy compared to AIS-based effort data. Incorporating frontal detection techniques enhances the representation of fine-scale oceanographic features, thereby improving the spatial agreement between predicted and observed fishing grounds. The application of dynamic time warping to chlorophyll-a forecasting improved real-time habitat predictions at a monthly scale. Furthermore, the spatial discrete choice model with spatially varying coefficients is applied to capture fishermen’s decision-making processes. The model reflects the climate-driven behavioral shifts, revealing eastward movement during El Niño and westward concentration during La Niña. These findings offer a potential tool for improving fishing efficiency and reducing carbon emissions. By connecting species distribution and vessel behavioral dynamics, this framework can offer scientific evidence for vessel day scheme planning and sustainable resource management in a dynamic marine environment.

presentations.presentation_title: Linear Trends in the M2 Tide in a Semi-enclosed Basin (Ariake Sea, Japan) Connected to the East China Sea: Role of Resonant Amplification and Energy Dissipation
presentations.abstract: In this study, we quantified linear trends in the amplitude (−0.185 m century−1, or −12.1% century−1 relative to the mean) and phase (−7.69° century−1) of M2 tidal elevation over the period 1970–2024 in the semi-enclosed Ariake Sea, along the eastern margin of the East China Sea (ECS). We applied a one-dimensional quarter-wavelength bay resonance model to separate the effects of the incoming M2 tide from the ECS and internal bay responses associated with resonance and bottom friction. A reduction in the bay resonance was detected after 1997, primarily as a result of the partial enclosure of Isahaya Bay, a sub-embayment of the Ariake Sea, by a dike. Furthermore, bottom friction and M2 energy dissipation were found to decrease, particularly after the 2000s, leading to an increase in the amplitude and a reduction in the phase lag of the M2 tide. We discuss how the less resonant condition and the weakening of the incoming M2 tide contributed to the recent decline in energy dissipation.
